📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to celebrity nicknames, is there any better than “JLo”? Jennifer Lopez’s moniker has been synonymous with her storied career for years. It’s been used in her music, it's her social media handle and has been used to name her fashion, fragrance and skincare lines. Although I just found out about how it started. Honestly, I’m so surprised this wasn’t common knowledge to me until today.

JLo has been JLo for over two decades. When the pop star, actress and businesswoman was recently asked about how she got it, here’s what she remarked:.

In a recent development, heavy D… Sony had Sony Studios down in Manhattan and everybody used to record in there. You could see all the Sony artists in there. And, Heavy would be in there, and he came by one day and I was recording, and I think I was recording my second album, the JLo album. And, I hadn’t named it the JLo album yet. And he came in and he was like, ‘What’s up Jenny Lo? JLo’s in the house.’ He just started calling me that, and I was like, ‘I think I’m gonna name my album JLo’.

Recent findings suggest that heavy D was a Jamaican-American rapper who had hits such as “Now That We Found Love”, “Got Me Waiting” and “We Got Our Own Thang” in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The rapper tragically died at the age of 44 of a pulmonary embolism back in 2011. As JLo recalled, Heavy D wasn’t only the first person to give her the nickname, it also inspired her to name her second album, J.Lo. When talking about the origin of the name, she also added this:.

I never expected it to stick the way it did. I just thought I was going to name the album JLo. And also, [rappers] started putting me in songs as Jennifer Lo, JLo, Jenny Lo. Like, it was a thing. I was already an actress, and I had already made my first record and that had hit, so now they knew who I was, and relationships that were kind of high profile, and they would write about us.

Sources indicate that the JLo album came out back in 2001, and the rest is history; she’s been JLo ever since. Along with the album title itself, Lopez noted that she also started being called the nickname in rap songs like Pitbull’s “Culo,” Jay-Z’s “Lost One”.

As she also mentioned, the nickname also got picked up when it came to tabloids writing about her famed relationships – like being one half of Bennifer of course. When JLo was married to Ben Affleck, she officially took his last name for a time, but she never stopped being JLo. And I can’t imagine the nickname ever going away for the superstar.

Sources indicate that the origins of JLo came up when she was on the Friends Keep Secrets podcast. Lopez is at the moment promoting her concert special, The JLo Show. The two-hour affair showcases JLo’s final performance at her Las Vegas residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace, which happened in March of this year. It's set to premiere on the 2026 TV schedule on November 26 at 8 p.m. on CBS and with a Paramount+ subscription.

The story of JLo's nickname is so random, but that’s why it’s such a good story. Sometimes you never know how one decision might change your whole career, which was the case with Jennifer Lopez and her JLo album.

Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio.
  • To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout.
  • Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means. Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

This is especially powerful for:.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Industry observers note that most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:.

Industry observers note that find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Recent findings suggest that customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

It has been revealed that recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

According to recent reports, A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We've been living in a world of mass entertainment dominated by superheroes and comic book characters for more than 25 years now, dating back to Marvel's earlier blockbuster hits like "X-Men" and "Spider-Man." Even small screen stuff like "The Walking Dead" has comic book roots.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

We've been living in a world of mass entertainment dominated by superheroes and comic book characters for more than 25 years now, dating back to Marvel's earlier blockbuster hits like "X-Men" and "Spider-Man." Even small screen stuff like "The Walking Dead" has comic book roots. But decades before any of that, an indie film pioneer made a superhero movie unlike any other.

Sources indicate that lloyd Kaufman is independent film, in many ways, as the founder of Troma Entertainment. His media empire was built on the backs of low-budget schlock like "Surf Nazis Must Die" and "Pterodactyl Woman from Beverly Hills," among many others. But Kaufman's defining hit came in 1984 in the form of "The Toxic Avenger," an ultra violent, campy, R-rated superhero affair. It remains a distinct piece of punk rock cinema more than 40 years removed, unmatched in its insanity by anything Marvel or DC has done on screen.

The movie takes place in the fictional town of Tromaville, known as the toxic waste capital of America. A bullied young janitor in a popular gym falls into a vat of toxic waste and turns into a super strong but disfigured man. He begins cleaning up the streets from evildoers in an often funny yet violent fashion.

"The Toxic Avenger" has a long history on screen and is now a cult legend, but that legend began in '84, at a time when superheroes were far from bankable fare in the mainstream. Co-directed by Michael Herz and Kaufman himself, the resulting movie can't be accused of being high art, but it's one heck of a wild swing, and a testament to what the indie filmmaking spirit can accomplish.

It has been revealed that at the time, Hollywood had only had the occasional superhero movie hit it big. "Superman: The Movie" in 1978 being the biggest one, while Batman didn't become a box office hero until 1989. Even that movie just led to the "Batman" franchise taking off rather than a broader trend of superheroes becoming big business. The '90s saw many try but few succeed, with stuff like "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles" more the exception rather than the rule.

All of this to say, when Lloyd Kaufman decided to make a dark superhero comedy — an R-rated and super violent one no less — it wasn't exactly a recipe for success. At least not on paper. But decades before "Deadpool" broke the Marvel mold by going R-rated and injecting comedy into the genre, "The Toxic Avenger" dared to venture into that territory.

It has been revealed that what's more, Kaufman and Co. did it on a shoestring budget of well under $1 million. "Deadpool" gets a lot of credit for being low-budget, but it still cost north of $50 million. What Kaufman pulled off with latex, old school special effects, and can-do indie spirit is nothing shy of impressive. Even those who are put off by the nature of this sort of exploitation film should be impressed by what was accomplished here with so little.

"The Toxic Avenger" has a demented sense of humor, and it doesn't give us a typical hero either. Toxie isn't a square-jawed, muscle-bound vigilante. He's a mutant who decides to clean up the streets with straight-up violence. The film has more in common with revenge driven horror/thrillers than it does any mainstream superhero movie. All the same, it became a cult hit and started a wildly unlikely franchise.

According to recent reports, "No theater would play it," Lloyd Kaufman remarked of "The Toxic Avenger" to Parallax View in 2010. "We couldn't get one theater to play it anywhere and then we took it to Cannes and not one deal. Nothing! And then a few months later we got one movie theater in Greenwich Village, New York, and there was a line around the theater.".

Recent findings suggest that that single theater paved the way for more to follow. This was also at the dawn of the VHS home video craze, which is where the movie really thrived — so much so that Kaufman eventually produced a series of sequels. That includes 1989's "The Toxic Avenger Part II" and "The Toxic Avenger Part III: The Last Temptation of Toxie," also released in '89. Much later, "Citizen Toxie: The Toxic Avenger IV" would arrive in 2000. A gore-soaked remake of "The Toxic Avenger" starring Peter Dinklage was also released in 2025.

Sources indicate that kaufman's crown jewel is an elbow grease style, gory, raunchy, rubber-suit take on superheroes that doesn't resemble anything we've seen in the 2000s, really. Sure, "Clayface" brought body horror to the DC Universe, but it's completely without a sense of humor. It's also slick and relatively expensive (for a horror movie).

Recent findings suggest that it was cutting edge then and it's impressively distinctive even now. More than that, "The Toxic Avenger" helped make the empire that is Troma. It's easy to write it all off as schlock, but Troma has been a haven for indie film for decades, with filmmakers like James Gunn ("Guardians of the Galaxy") cutting their teeth there. Without this movie, who knows if the empire as we know it even exists?

You can grab "The Toxic Avenger" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

Dancing With the Stars pro Jan Ravnik has fanned the flames of his ongoing feud with Maks Chmerkovskiy.

After Ravnik, 31, was told during a live backstage interview about his Tuesday, November 17, performances with partner Tatyana Ali, that his waltz was “beautiful,” he replied, “say that to Maks,” and pointed a directive finger towards the camera.

The professional dancer was joined by fellow pro Alan Bersten for the interview, with Bersten, 32, flashing a shocked face to the camera as he took in Ravnik’s cheeky remark.

The livestream moment was shared via a fan’s X account that night with the comments, “Ahhhhh not @JAnRavnik throwing shade at Maks !!!!!” and “Thank you to the person who caught this on TikTok.”.

Ravnik’s comment comes after seemingly several barbs were recently sent back and forth between himself and Chmerkovskiy, 46, who have locked horns since October 2025 after Chmerkovskiy criticized Ravnik’s debut DWTS season.

Social media customers reported online ahead of the Tuesday, November 10, episode of DWTS that Chmerkovskiy and fellow pro Gleb Savchenko had allegedly placed bets via a sports betting platform that Ali, 47, and Ravnik would be eliminated at the end of the night’s episode.

During an interview with USA Today after the episode wrapped, Ravnik noted his anthem for this season of DWTS was Taylor Swift’s “The Smallest Man Who Ever Lived,” before raising his eyebrows for the camera.

The response sparked online fan speculation that he was referring to Chmerkovskiy.

According to recent reports, in addition to comments made by Ravnik during Tuesday’s livestream, a post-episode interview with USA Today also seemingly referred to the betting drama. When asked for a message for fans, Ravnik remarked, “I hope you lose all your money,” which stopped Ali in her tracks.

“Well, OK, that was more of a general question but we got very specific,” she noted as Ravnik fell back in a fit of giggles.

During the October 24, 2025 episode of Chmerkovskiy’s wife, Peta Murgatroyd’s “Penthouse With Peta” podcast, Chmerkovskiy said, “I’m sorry, Jan has absolutely no business being a pro on Dancing With the Stars,” adding that Ravnik had “zero foundation technique, quality [and] understanding of the partnership.”.

Ravnik responded three days later with a TikTok captioned “Me When Anyone Talks Trash About Jan,” and, despite an apology from Chmerkovskiy over his initial comments, a subtle war of words has endured ever since.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

Industry observers note that it also has a removable lens cover to block the camera’s view, which is a nice privacy perk, though closing the cover doesn’t turn off the microphone. For complete audio privacy, you need to disable the microphone in the Ring app.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid blueprint, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

It has been revealed that at these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lifestyle influencer Emilie Kiser has shared her heartbreak as she prepares to mark one-and-a-half years since the death of her son, Trigg.

“Bawled the whole way home from my hair appointment, just missing my Triggy so so much,” Kiser, 27, wrote over a Tuesday, November 17, Instagram Story photo that revealed her sitting in her car as tears streamed down her face. “I’m just so f***ing sad … tomorrow if a year and a half since we’ve lost Trigg and I just, literally, can’t even believe it.”.

The social media personality, who announced in July that she is pregnant after the May 2025 death of Trigg, 3, following a fall into the family’s backyard pool, added that the reality of the milestone had hit her earlier in the week.

“It already has hit me, this entire week, but … it’s so painful, and just so s***ty,” she mentioned.

A subsequent Instagram Story featured a photo of Kiser’s reddened face as she stared blankly ahead. “I genuinely hate making others uncomfortable, like, sometimes that’s how I feel crying in front of people or it being noticeable that I’ve been crying,” she wrote over the top of it. “So now avoiding going into my home because I have contractors here.”.

An earlier Instagram Story had explained that despite the sunny disposition she often exhibits via her social media posts, “social media is fake sometimes.” She added that she wasn’t immune from “masking how I really feel” and explained that it’s how she survives “most days so my brain doesn’t completely shut down.”.

Sources indicate that kiser and her husband, Brady Kiser, lost their child at their Arizona home on May 12, 2025. Brady, 30, and Trigg’s brother Teddy, 19 months, were both home when Trigg was pulled unconscious from the pool.

Police officers arrived at the scene and began performing CPR before firefighters took over life-saving measures. Trigg was subsequently flown to Phoenix Children’s Hospital for further treatment and the Chandler, Arizona, Police Department confirmed to Us on May 18, 2025, that Trigg died.

Check our latest news in Google News.

Check our latest news in Apple News.

Sources indicate that on August 28 that year, Emilie broke her silence on the tragedy. “Loss of this magnitude feels impossible to put into words. I’ve spent days, weeks, months trying to find them and also take the time I’ve needed to digest the loss of my baby,” she wrote via social media at the time.

According to recent reports, she confirmed her current pregnancy via Instagram on July 3. “We are so grateful and excited to share that we will be welcoming another baby into our family 🤍🪿. This news feels very surreal and has already been such a bright light to us during some of our darkest days,” Emilie wrote at the time. “As I stated last year, my family’s privacy will always be my priority. Because of that, I’m not sure how much I will be sharing about this pregnancy and next phase of life, but I appreciate your understanding as I navigate those boundaries.”.

  • An HBO show that got the world talking from the moment it debuted, the post-apocalyptic drama started by following Joel (Pedro Pascal) as he escorted the teenage Ellie (Bella Ramsey) across a devastated United States ravaged by a fungal infection that had turned people into violent creatures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Last of Us is a TV show that has meant a lot to a lot of people, as it has successfully translated the emotional core of the hugely popular video game and built on the complexity of the character relationships. The final season, anticipated to debut in 2027, is sure to be emotional for fans, too. So it’s not at all surprising to hear that the cast is emotional as they get to the end of filming and will have to say goodbye to each other.

An HBO show that got the world talking from the moment it debuted, the post-apocalyptic drama started by following Joel (Pedro Pascal) as he escorted the teenage Ellie (Bella Ramsey) across a devastated United States ravaged by a fungal infection that had turned people into violent creatures. With Season 3 delving deeper into the journey of Joel’s brother, Tommy Miller, actor Gabriel Luna not only has to say goodbye to a character he’ll know much better, but he’ll also be leaving the cast and crew behind after bidding them an emotional farewell. Here’s what he told Entertainment Weekly about the emotions that are already starting to swirl:.

In a recent development, oh man, a lot of emotions are going around. But right now I think we’re all too tired to feel them. [Laughs.] Because it’s just massive. Obviously I can’t give anything away, but people who’ve played the game know the level of the scope of what we’re dealing with here towards the end of the story. I’m so proud of Bella [Ramsey], Kaitlyn [Dever], and Kyriana [Kratter], who’s joined the cast, for being the tip of the spear and shouldering the weight of this production and what it requires from them.

If you played The Last of Us games, you knew that Abby would be seen on the show as a villain after killing Pedro Pascal's Joel. No matter her motivation or the extent of her own trauma, it would be challenging for viewers to understand the actions of someone taking out such a beloved character. And then, the Season 2 finale ended with the focus shifting to Kaitlyn Dever's Abby, who will take center stage in The Last of Us Season 3.

Industry observers note that in a world like the one portrayed in The Last of Us, where everything is heightened as you just try to survive and not get killed or infected, emotions understandably run high for the cast helping bring that world to life. And even though Tommy comes in and out of the story, The Terminal List actor can’t help but be impressed by how the Ellie, Abby, and Lev actors are handling everything required of them, as they head closer to the finish line. He went on to say:.

The bulk of my work was back in the summer, and then I’d go back and forth and come in for two, three weeks of time, but they’re here every day and doing the lion’s share of the work.

Recent findings suggest that since the Naughty Dog video game-turned-TV series is a massive production, it sounds like there’s going to be a prolonged series of goodbyes taking place as storylines are wrapped up and actors depart. Gabriel Luna not only has to process the emotion of saying goodbye to his own character and wrapping up a story that he likely feels very connected to after three seasons, but he also has to handle the departure of each of his co-stars. That’s a lot of emotions for the Dexter: Resurrection star, who will probably be exhausted by the time it’s all remarked and done. He pretty much said just that:.

It has been revealed that we’re getting to the end of it, and people are starting to wrap, and we’re giving them their flowers, and then they’re heading off, and one by one, the family is dwindling down to just the final few. We’re about to get a welcomed break and respite from what we’ve been doing, and then we have to come back and finish strong after the holiday. We’re so excited for this thing to come out.

According to recent reports, I can only imagine the tears that will be flowing and the emotions that will be felt as the final days of the HBO series come to an end, and everyone says their final goodbyes. Fans anxiously anticipating the third season will have to pack their patience pants while waiting for details on when it will officially premiere. In the meantime, the first two seasons of The Last of Us are streaming with an HBO Max subscription.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • "The Social Reckoning" is finally hitting the home market.
  • In case you're unfamiliar with "The Social Reckoning" writ large, here's the gist.
  • Industry observers note that fail it did, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"The Social Reckoning" is finally hitting the home market. It will become available to buy or rent on digital starting November 24, 2026, prior to its physical media release on January 12, 2027.

In case you're unfamiliar with "The Social Reckoning" writ large, here's the gist. Almost two decades after he won an Academy Award for writing the screenplay for "The Social Network," a 2010 dramatization of the founding of Facebook directed by David Fincher, Aaron Sorkin decided to make a sequel that focuses on what Facebook has become in the 2020s. Jesse Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar nod for playing Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Network," declined to return to the role and was replaced by "Succession" veteran, Emmy and Tony winner, and Sorkin's "The Trial of the Chicago 7" collaborator Jeremy Strong. With Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Betty Gilpin, and Billy Magnussen starring alongside Strong, the project seemed almost too big to fail before it premiered in theaters on October 9, 2026.

Industry observers note that fail it did, though. Though it reportedly only lost a couple million for Sony (per Deadline), the film absolutely underperformed at the box office, and its rating on Rotten Tomatoes is a middling-to-bleak 54%. So what happened here? Well, from my perspective, "The Social Reckoning" is just a bad movie ... and /Film's chief film critic Chris Evangelista agrees with me. What went wrong as Sorkin tried to make a legacy sequel to one of the best films of the 21st century? Quite a lot actually!

Sources indicate that I'll circle back to the "Social Network" of it all shortly, but the bottom line here is that "The Social Reckoning" just ... stinks to high heaven. From the embarrassing prologue featuring Portia Doubleday as a caricature named Kayleigh (I'm not kidding) to the fact that Aaron Sorkin keeps forcing Oscar winner Mikey Madison into outfits that would make her title character from "Anora" blush (in the name of corporate espionage), I found "The Social Network" to be a uniformly dreadful watch from start to finish. Not only is the script clunky as all hell — unfortunately, an ongoing problem with many of Sorkin's recent screenplays — but the story is attempting to make some sort of larger point that doesn't just fall flat but thuds directly to the floor. We already know social media makes everyone angry and insane, and we also know that social media has contributed to right-wing radicalization. Sorkin making a movie that beats us over the head with these two ideas and also ends in a full recreation of the January 6, 2021 insurrection is just as bad as it sounds in theory.

Sources indicate that it's also incredible to me that Sorkin managed to cast a lot of great actors and coach them into giving some of the worst performances of their careers. Madison is an enigmatic and compelling performer, and Sorkin transforms her into the robotic Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, a deeply unlikable person who doesn't seem to understand human behavior. Jeremy Allen White's journalist Jeff Horwitz is nothing but an exposition machine, and Jeremy Strong's Mark Zuckerberg has no interiority and sounds like Kermit the Frog. The only person who's good in this movie is Bill Burr. Think about that for a second.

"The Social Network" might be one of my very favorite movies of all time, but I can tell you, from a completely unbiased perspective, that "The Social Reckoning" is a wholly undeserving sequel to that 2010 masterpiece. It's clear now, with plenty of hindsight and movies like this, that "The Social Network" was good because of director David Fincher and despite Sorkin. To be fair to Sorkin, he basically admitted that to The Hollywood Reporter after "The Social Reckoning" got soundly panned.

It has been revealed that "I would have rather David Fincher directed it — I would rather David Fincher direct everything — but David has an exclusive deal at Netflix, and this was owned by Sony," Sorkin told the outlet on their "Awards Chatter" podcast. Not only did Sorkin also admit that he's "very worried that the parts of directing that [he's] not good at are those parts that you can't learn," he also said, "I was surprised by how little of the science of filmmaking I'd managed to absorb [from other directors] ... I have no visual sensibility, it turns out.".

I have to agree with him. Despite the same cinematographer — Jeff Cronenweth — working on both "Network" and "Reckoning," the sequel is visually bland, unimaginatively shot, and even recycles a couple reaction and establishing shots throughout its run time. Basically, "The Social Reckoning" is a poorly made film that I cannot in good conscience recommend; in fact, I'd recommend you just watch "The Social Network" instead. But if you're still interested, you can check out "The Social Reckoning" at home once it's available.

Tech Report: Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Tech giant Is Stepping In

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Big smartphones have long been the norm.
  • Sources indicate that despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller.
  • While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a newly introduced iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Sources indicate that despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a newly introduced iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough.".

Enough Phone really does seem small. The manufacturer says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it prepares to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current blueprint is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

According to recent reports, enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough states this device "should last you into the next decade.".

In a recent development, now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is right now in the prototype stage. Enough notes that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company presently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the manufacturer's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

8 Funniest 'Far Side' Comics Starring Cowboys

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gary Larson, the comedy genius behind The Far Side comic strip, loved to turn things into their opposites.
  • Sometimes he made them just plain weird, which Larson did with everything.
  • Here are eight of the funniest Far Side comics about cowboys, who are portrayed quite differently than they were in the typical Clint Eastwood or John Wayne movie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gary Larson, the comedy genius behind The Far Side comic strip, loved to turn things into their opposites. Serious, brilliant scientists were cast as childish dummies who drop everything when they hear an ice cream truck pass by. Simple-minded cows could be so smart that they plot the deaths of their owners. As for cowboys, the manly men of the Old West, Larson loved to portray them as meek and cowardly.

Sometimes he made them just plain weird, which Larson did with everything.

Here are eight of the funniest Far Side comics about cowboys, who are portrayed quite differently than they were in the typical Clint Eastwood or John Wayne movie.

This comic strip is a great example of Larson’s love of turning popular trends and tropes upside down. The adorable bunnies, armed with revolvers, have taken over the stagecoach with two Old West cowboys. The funniest part about the predicament, though, is the one cowboy’s concern for how this is going to look on their official report.

Being the fastest gunslinger in town was a point of pride for cowboys—or at least for the cowboys in the movies I’ve seen— so the idea of a gunman being so slow that he loses to a sloth is especially hilarious.

This comic strip feels like it’s a play on this classic Clint Eastwood movie line, "You've got to ask yourself one question: 'Do I feel lucky?'".

To be clear, this didn’t come from a Clint Eastwood Western. It’s actually from Dirty Harry, which is a movie where Eastwood plays a cop instead. Still, Eastwood’s strong ties to Western films make this line ripe for parody in a Western setting.

For the record, it seems that, in this comic strip, Bart has literally never been lucky in his life, having lost a leg, an eye, a hand, and having been shot through his hat many times. I mean, perhaps he’s lucky he hasn’t died, but it feels like being super lucky would have protected him from getting shot at all.

In a recent development, tattling is never a tough-guy thing to do, which is why this comic is so funny. It shows one cowboy squealing on another, telling on him for having stated a discouraging word. This, of course, is a play on the old folk song “Home on the Range,” which has the lyric “Where seldom is heard a discouraging word.”.

This one is just incredibly weird, but still incredibly funny. These cowboys are comparing how tiny their horses are, which they keep in little jars. It is such a strange image, but that's where the comedy comes from.

Honestly, I would have loved to see this acted out by some famous western star like Clint Eastwood or John Wayne or someone like that.

This type of joke isn’t specific to cowboys, but it’s the kind of thing Larson did a lot with The Far Side, which was to take a common expression and interpret it in the most literal way possible. For the old cowboy threat “This town ain’t big enough for the both of us,” Larson portrayed two gunslingers in a tiny little town of dollhouse-sized buildings.

Another example of Larson being overly literal is this comic strip. It is a common trope in Westerns for a hero to ride off into the sunset. Only Larson could turn that into a charred cowboy who actually rode into the sun.

Recent findings suggest that this one isn’t about opposites or about cowboys being weirdos, but it’s the funniest-ever Far Side comic about cowboys by virtue of being a shockingly dark joke. Only Gary Larson could make the punchline to a comic strip a pile of dead horses. It’s hard to imagine Charles Schulz or Jim Davis ever doing such a thing. But that’s what made The Far Side so funny, because it didn't follow the rules of other comic strips.

Who Killed Fashion Founders Bryan Walker and Michelle Min?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases.
  • In a recent development, “I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker.
  • According to recent reports, by the time paramedics arrived, Walker and Min were dead from what OPD assistant chief Casey Johnson characterized as “apparent gunshots” in a press conference later that day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases. Century-old homes by brand-name architects like Bernard Maybeck and Walter Steilberg dot the incline, which straddles the border of Berkeley and Oakland. Each residence is worth millions; increase the amount for the occasional bit of newer construction. Unlike the busy urban streets below, the area is incredibly quiet. That’s one of the reasons everyone heard the shots.

In a recent development, “I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker. The couple, creators of the Bryn Walker clothing brand, were found just outside their residence around 10:45 a.m. on October 2, 2026, shortly after neighbors called 911 to report the sound of gunfire. Initial confusion about jurisdiction sent police from both Berkeley’s and Oakland’s departments to the scene.

According to recent reports, by the time paramedics arrived, Walker and Min were dead from what OPD assistant chief Casey Johnson characterized as “apparent gunshots” in a press conference later that day. A firearm, he said, was located at the scene. He declined to offer further details on the case, saying that the department’s homicide division would handle the investigation.

Industry observers note that nearly seven weeks later, we still know next to nothing about how Walker and Min died. While OPD turned down my request to speak with Johnson, it sent me a press release with the same details he laid out on October 2. Follow-up questions were met with: “There are no updates being released other than the information below.”.

Bryn Walker store on Vine Street in Berkeley, California.

“I don’t know what has publicly been shared or what privately has been learned about what took place,” Salzman states carefully. Police have been silent since the brief press conference the day the bodies were discovered. But Michelle Min’s brother, Paul Min, hasn’t been quiet.

Sources indicate that within two days after his 63-year-old sister was found dead, Paul spoke with outlets including the LA Times and the California Post, accusing his brother-in-law of killing his wife, then himself, following a series of disastrous financial decisions that led to significant losses and a collapse in his mental state. The interviews, given so soon after the crime, suggest Paul was still in a state of shock over his loss. Walker, who was 61 when he died, was “the most honest, responsible, hardworking guy you have ever known,” Paul told the LA Times. “I loved him like a brother.” Michelle “was utterly devoted to Bryan to the very end,” Paul told the Post, “and he shot her.”.

After those interviews, which were published that first weekend in October, Paul fell silent too; I made multiple efforts to arrange an interview but was ultimately unsuccessful. But according to the Post’s interview, Walker “had quietly taken out loans against their properties, and had gambled on risky options and leveraged positions,” with estimated losses of “well over $100 million.” The debt, per the LA Times story, allegedly prompted Walker to suggest that he and the Min siblings “end things”—a proposal that alarmed the Mins, but only because of its implications for Walker’s mental health. Paul didn’t see Walker as a danger: “He said the idea that Walker would or could harm them was absurd to the two of them,” reported the Times.

The Mins came to the US from Korea in 1977, settling first near Kansas City. Michelle met Walker there in the 1980s, and after the Mins’ parents chose to move to California, the siblings, and Walker, followed. In 1992 the couple opened a clothing store in Berkeley that sold goods from other makers. As time went on, they began to manufacture more and more of their own goods.

Eventually, Bryn Walker evolved into a clothing brand known for loose linen looks with an Asian-meets-Swedish flair. “Flowy, a touch eclectic, made for perhaps older women who want to mesh elegant/sophisticated with a bit of boho uniqueness,” a longtime Berkeley resident told me over email. “Women who want to look expensive but with a bit of verve.” When I described the manufacturer to one San Francisco resident as “elevated Chico’s,” I got a stern look. “You better not let any of the Bryn Walker moms at Lowell hear you say that,” she remarked, referencing the city’s hotly competitive public high school. “These are not humorous people.”.

Bryn Walker store on Fourth Street in Berkeley, California.

Industry observers note that according to the Post piece, Walker “had stepped aside and allowed his designer wife to control their mutual business and his eponymous fashion label,” but it’s not clear when that management change occurred. As the brand grew, it struck a chord with fashion businesses across the country—from luxury boutiques to the family-run department store chain Dillard’s. Bryn Walker also opened its own brick-and-mortar storefronts beyond Berkeley.

It has been revealed that many of those stores are now gone. One Bryn Walker location in Santa Monica closed prior to mid-March of 2021, while a 22-year-old outpost in Palo Alto shuttered in 2020. On the East Coast, a shop in Edgartown, on Martha’s Vineyard, went dark in 2024. A call to its shop in Vineyard Haven was met with a recorded message saying the business would be closed until further notice. That leaves just two tech giant-owned shops, both in Berkeley, where Bryn Walker began.

One of those stores is on Berkeley’s buzzy Fourth Street, a glossy shopping destination lined with outposts of national brands like Apple, Lululemon, and Herman Miller. With items generally priced between $130–$300, it fits right into the overall ethos of that street—and Berkeley—where almost everything is spendy but not flashy; theoretically accessible, though not to those on a budget. During my recent visit to the shop, the sole staffer remained pleasant even after I identified myself as a journalist—but her tone grew firm. “It’s all still too raw,” she mentioned of the tragedy.

I asked if, as he’d said he would in his Post interview, Paul Min had taken over management of the manufacturer following its founders’ deaths. “I don’t know about that,” she replied, before declining to speak further. I was told by another local business owner that Bryn Walker employees are actively seeking other employment; it’s unclear what will happen to the label now that its creators are gone. I tried to reach Bryn Walker management by phone and email for this story, but did not receive a response.

Sources indicate that emilie Raguso was one of the first journalists to report on the deaths, for her independent outlet, The Berkeley Scanner. As she began investigating, she “saw that the number of open shops was different based on where you looked,” she says. “I was getting this early inkling of what others later reported as far as the business being in trouble.”.

“The writing was on the wall,” she continues, “but there was nothing explicit. It did seem like, Oh, this is not a thriving business.”.

Paul’s comments to the media didn’t address the health of the business. Instead, he was focused on Walker and Michelle’s personal finances, which he alleged were laid to waste by Walker’s mismanagement. “Your spouse lied to you and lost over $100 million and you might be out on the streets,” Paul told the Post. “You might go from being one of the wealthiest people in the country to being homeless because your husband lied to you and wagered everything on crazy bets.”.

According to Paul, things grew so grim for Walker that the Mins spoke about institutionalizing him. But it’s also unclear how they would have acted on that without Walker’s cooperation. California enacted its CARE Court program in 2023, more easily allowing court-ordered treatment plans for those who might pose a threat to themselves or others. But in practice, courts have been reluctant to take that drastic step, frequently rejecting petitions from those closest to the person in crisis.

Bryn Walker-Pacific Cotton store on Main Street in Vineyard Haven, Massachusetts.

In a recent development, speaking with the LA Times, Paul stated that in Walker and Michelle’s home, he “found a note that lists a couple of [mental health] facilities. I speculate he saw that note or somehow figured out she was going to institutionalize him, but I have no idea.”.

Recent findings suggest that paul’s claim that Walker killed Michelle over snowballing financial fears isn’t out of the realm of possibility, even in a place as wealthy as the Bay Area. One year before Walker and Michelle died, almost to the day, entrepreneur Paula Truong fatally shot her husband, Thomas, and their daughters, Mackenzie and Alexandra, before hanging herself in the garage of their $2.2 million San Francisco home. Reporting found that the family had experienced a string of financial challenges, including several failed business ventures, a home foreclosure, and a number of unpaid debts.

According to recent reports, but that was in San Francisco—a sometimes gritty city that people escape with moves to places like Panoramic Hill. “When you get up into the hills, it does feel like a world apart,” Raguso notes. “It feels insulated from a lot of the more common disturbances and things that we deal with down on the flatlands.”.

Salzman has lived on that hill for more than 20 years, and she’s still struggling with the notion that her neighbor might have killed his wife. “Bryan was very engaged with neighbors who were needing support that were near him,” she says, characterizing him and Michelle as “committed to the community.” But she also believes that the fear of losing wealth can drive people to desperate acts. “We see wealth as being both our greatest need and our greatest opportunity here,” she says, “and we are told that we will be happy when we consume. This is the message that we’re given everywhere we look”—especially in a region with more billionaires than anywhere else in the world.

It has been revealed that raguso isn’t sure why Oakland police are taking so long to announce the results of their investigation. “At some point, there would be a ruling,” she says, citing possible delays with the medical examiner’s office as a reason things haven’t been resolved. According to Salzman, the vacuum of information has inspired her to look at all her neighbors with a little more care. “Part of what I awoke to was how little I know about really what’s going on with people that I’m geographically so close to,” she says.

Sources indicate that “I just would have loved for there to have been a way to be a part of showing up for them, even around the little things. The more people that are aware of what is happening, the more people are potentially able to heal.”.

Are we going to see "28 Years Later: Part III?" Director Danny Boyle is certainly interested in doing it and Alex Garland has written a script. The problem? Money. This year's "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" finally delivered the moment fans have been waiting for, bringing back Cillian Murphy as Jim. It was a small appearance teeing up something much larger in a presumed third installment. As Boyle recently explained, that movie is only going to happen if they can find the money.

In a recent development, speaking recently with Deadline during an event for his upcoming movie "Ink," Boyle's tabloid media origin story that will make you feel sick, the Oscar-winning director addressed the status of the third and presumably final entry in the "28" franchise. "There is a strategy for a third part of '28 Years Later.' Alex has written a fantastic script," Boyle noted. "We gotta raise the money to make it.".

Sony Pictures produced both "28 Years Later" and "The Bone Temple." And while "28 Years Later" killed it at the box office, the sequel didn't. That's why Sony isn't eager to give it the green light. Speaking further, Boyle said that the third installment would bring the whole franchise to a close:.

"[Cillian Murphy]'s up for it, and it's a fantastic part. Alex has written this fantastic part for him. Those of you who saw 'The Bone Temple,' the second part to '28 Years Later,' he's teased at the end of that. The third film does complete the story in a beautiful, mathematically perfect way, in which the circle is closed.".

Sources indicate that creatively speaking, critics and audiences generally agreed that both of the recent "28" movies were damn good. But Hollywood is a business and money became an issue pretty rapidly. "28 Years Later" made $151 million against a budget in the $60 million range. That was good enough. "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" flopped at the box office though, bringing in just $58.5 million worldwide on a similar budget. Unfortunately, the math doesn't math for anyone who wants to make money in this business.

That's why "28 Years Later: Part III" probably won't happen. Admittedly, "probably" is doing some heavy lifting there. Cillian Murphy is an Oscar-winning actor for his work in "Oppenheimer," Danny Boyle is an Oscar-winning director, and Alex Garland is an Oscar-nominated screenwriter. It's a powerhouse team. That makes it unlikely but not impossible.

Sources indicate that the most realistic path to getting it made would be partnering with a streaming service. Netflix is releasing Boyle's new movie "Ink" and the streamer also has a partnership with Sony. That would be the logical choice. But if Boyle and Garland want it as a more traditional theatrical release? That's where it gets more complicated and far less likely.

As for where it all went wrong? The bonkers ending in "28 Years Later" left audiences divided, for one. There was also a very short, roughly six-month gap between installments, which seemingly hurt more than it helped. But playing Monday morning quarterback doesn't help now. It's really about Boyle and co. getting creative to see if they can cobble together the money to bring this story to a close.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you know how everyone is debating whether smoking is back?
  • Sources indicate that the brand’s late-30s founder, Michelle Duncan, doesn’t smoke herself and doesn’t do barely there makeup along the lines of Rhode, Rare Beauty, or Glossier.
  • Duncan knew the industry she was getting into.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you know how everyone is debating whether smoking is back? Atlas Atelier is like the subject of the makeup version of that conversation, in both its long, skinny lipsticks that evoke a cheeky cigarette and its past-bedtime, maybe something a little naughty is happening vibe. The Paris-based brand makes just lipstick, blush, and a black liquid eyeliner, all engineered to be best shown off at night, maybe under the light of candles, or as you sip a cocktail or wear a jacket with strong shoulders. It’s makeup that is supposed to look like makeup. Severe is not too strong a word to use.

Sources indicate that the brand’s late-30s founder, Michelle Duncan, doesn’t smoke herself and doesn’t do barely there makeup along the lines of Rhode, Rare Beauty, or Glossier. “I am a Fresh Yorker, and I’ve been living in Paris primarily for the last four or five years. When I arrived in Paris, everyone was so well-heeled that you would never see somebody wearing a gym look to go to dinner. This resonated with me about this idea of dressing up to go out no matter what you were doing, even if it’s going to a café. That was a huge inspiration for me,” she indicates.

Duncan knew the industry she was getting into. She’s a veteran of brands owned by Estée Lauder, including both MAC and Tom Ford Beauty, and she also worked for Cartier. Atlas Atelier—the “atlas” is in homage to Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged—just came out this fall in the US (now available at Violet Grey and Bergdorf Goodman). Vanity Fair spoke to Duncan about Paris expat life, rejecting celebrity brands, and what happens to makeup in unstable times.

The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: You know the challenges of the beauty industry. You’re not an influencer; you didn’t pick a celebrity to be the face of the brand or to partner with. Why not make it easier on yourself?

Michelle Duncan: Friends will ask, “Didn’t you want to do this with a celeb?” I wouldn’t want to. Culture and society is so focused on a quick buck right this second, which I’m totally into. I love making money very fast. This is so much about the world of Atlas, with the packaging and with the storytelling. The brand ethos of Atlas is about the night, about this seductive environment that, to me, will actually cut through the clutter in a long-term way. When a high-profile person launches a brand, the bet that they’re taking is on who they are as a person. For me, the bet is, do you buy into Atlas’s story?

Industry observers note that makeup has gotten very big and plastic and in some ways looks like toys. That was sort of my first remit on it. The whole brief was: We want to create something that looks like an object that you want to be able to keep. My inspirations really are the 1930s, the Art Deco, Paris moment, and how do we make it leap into the ’80s in some ways because that’s obviously also just a second extension of the ’30s?

The 1980s version of Art Deco is so good. All that lacquer and glass blocks and chrome lamps.

It felt like something that was radically different from what’s going on in the world right now, at least in beauty land. We’re exiting this no-makeup era, or hopefully exiting this quiet-luxury era. Those things were very pared back. Maybe focusing more internally about wellness and things like that. I understood that this was missing and that it was going to come back.

The idea of self-expression in a sort of glamorous way. In the 1930s, it was not a great time in the world. And if we remember, the 1980s in New York City was decadent and over the top and seemed very fun, but as a reaction to what was going on. I would argue that we are kind of in that place right now. We don’t really need to go into politics, but it is chaos right now. And so the answer to that is always this other form of self-expression.

Sources indicate that the name of the brand is a reference to Atlas Shrugged. Are you a substantial fan of Ayn Rand?

I’ve always admired and been inspired by Dagny Taggart, one of the most iconic characters in 20th-century literature. She’s written as a fiercely independent entrepreneur in a male-dominated world, who is in control of her own life and embracing its complexity. When creating my business, I was trying to channel that vision of what a woman can be: intellectually formidable, professionally ambitious, and comfortable with her sensuality. I was especially struck by one moment in the novel, when Dagny draws on a statue using her lipstick, reminding us that makeup isn’t just to change our appearance—it can be a tool for women to own their own power. I wanted to create a makeup line that gave women that same feeling of confidence, ambition, and sensuality through tools like lipstick, blush, and eyeliner.

Were you a makeup lover growing up?

Sources indicate that yes. I have been wearing this winged-eyeliner situation for a very long time. Actually, since I was a teenager. If I don’t have my eyeliner on, I feel naked and I don’t feel like I have everything with me.

So you’re wearing eyeliner at home. What about the people who are reading this who may be thinking, I never go out, or I have kids, or I’m tired, or I work a lot, or all of those things? Do you want people to go out a lot? Do you go out a lot? Is it more just the mindset of going out at nighttime?

Recent findings suggest that the idea of my brand is it should be a pleasure to put on makeup, and I want people to experience pleasure again and just forget about all of the things that are happening, like picking up the kids, or going to the grocery store, or getting the dry cleaning, or whatever it is. Just remembering what it means to have a nice time and be inspired by the night. I, on purpose and by design, did not launch foundations or these technical components of makeup, because that’s just not really what it’s about.

According to recent reports, how is expat life? I know so many people who have moved to France, or they would love to move to France. What do you think that’s about?

In my social circle, it tends to consist of either people somehow in the fashion industry, the music industry, or the arts communities. A lot of those industries have just become quite commercial in America, as an example. And I haven’t lived in a lot of other countries, so I don’t really know expat life so well. But the amount of Italians that are here, the Spanish, the Germans, the Americans, and everyone just has this chaotic, frenetic energy of being around each other and doing things together. It’s pretty remarkable.

I know you’re not doing celebrity spokespeople, but who would you want if you didn’t have to think about money or access or if they already had a beauty contract?

Recent findings suggest that somebody like [the artist] Nadia Lee Cohen. She’s super glamorous. She’s quite creative. She’s a genius in a lot of ways, and she actually uses makeup as art. And then somebody like Dakota Johnson. I think she’s so chic now. Dua Lipa. I love her. She’s got the perfect energy for this. She’s there, she’s having a good time, and she’s powerful.

Do you want to expand into other products ? It feels like you could do a fragrance. Or maybe a very chic makeup remover?

I can’t wait for the day that we are able to launch a fragrance because that is one of those things you remember, along with lip color. You remember what they smell like, and when they leave the room, and so that’s the impression that Atlas is supposed to be giving—you’re remembered when you left the room.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Now that Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, Amazon MGM's looks for the franchise are coming together.
  • Industry observers note that in an interview with GQ, the "Dune" director was asked what he looks for in a 007 actor.
  • It has been revealed that denis Villeneuve unpacks the process of casting the newest James Bond: Robert Pattinson.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Now that Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, Amazon MGM's looks for the franchise are coming together. The newly introduced owners of the Bond IP are clearly sparing no expense for the upcoming "Bond 26," hiring a major director in Denis Villeneuve to shepherd the project, which will now be led by one of the biggest names in Hollywood. After the missteps that were Daniel Craig's last few films in the tux, it seems Amazon is aiming to re-establish Bond movies as must-see cinematic events. For Villeneuve, however, the star power of his Bond actor is less notable than the ability to project the energy of a cold-blooded killer.

Industry observers note that in an interview with GQ, the "Dune" director was asked what he looks for in a 007 actor. "A first quality is that I need to believe that this man is a killer," he replied. "Because more than a spy, Bond is an assassin, and I need that kind of strength. I need that kind of anger deep in the eye. It's not everybody who has that." Those who doubt whether Pattinson can do so need only take a glance at the casting announcement video, in which the actor's Bond emerges from the darkness aiming his Walther PPK and wearing a cold, resolute expression on his face. There's a definite edge to his brief appearance in the clip, and you can see why Villeneuve was impressed.

It has been revealed that denis Villeneuve unpacks the process of casting the newest James Bond: Robert Pattinson. https://t.co/DLgqqUErYa pic.twitter.com/FWB1l6r2L8.

— GQ Magazine (@GQMagazine) November 17, 2026.

That said, it seems Pattinson wasn't actually the first choice for Bond. According to a recent report, Villeneuve initially settled on "Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery" actor Josh O'Connor, who ultimately dropped out and cleared the way for Pattinson. But that will almost certainly prove to be a positive thing.

According to recent reports, robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of the franchise introducing audiences to relative unknowns in the lead role. But that's a good thing, as Bond is in need of revitalization following the debacle that was 2021's "No Time to Die." Pattinson's star power will help restore the franchise's popularity. But the "Batman" star is more than just an A-lister with a built-in audience. He's easily one of the most talented actors of his generation, having demonstrated an extraordinary ability to completely transform on-screen. As Bond, he'll no doubt exude exactly the kind of subtly sinister energy Denis Villeneuve is looking for and which has been one of the most vital aspects of the character since his introduction.

In 1962, "Dr. No" kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise by introducing audiences to Sean Connery in the lead role. Rather than casting an established star with the kind of refined energy you'd expect of a gentleman spy, producers Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman hired a working class former footballer from Scotland, and it was a masterstroke. 007 debuted on the massive screen with an edge that only Connery could bring to the role, and that's been an integral aspect of the cinematic incarnation of the character ever since. Sure, director Terence Young helped round off some of Connery's rough edges, but he'd be nothing without the sense of danger the Scotsman brought to the screen. Thankfully, it seems both Villeneuve and Pattinson recognize that, and it's yet another aspect of this casting that bodes well for "Bond 26.".

According to recent reports, denis Villeneuve clearly values the killer instinct aspect of James Bond above everything else. But the director has plenty of other requirements for the role. As he went on to tell GQ, "I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache, someone that [...] when he comes into the room everything starts to gravitate around him, that kind of strong charisma." It's a foundational aspect of Bond and a characteristic every actor to portray the spy has possessed. But that's not all Villeneuve is looking for.

In a recent development, the French-Canadian filmmaker went on to say he also looks for "sensuality" in his Bond actor, as well as "dark humor" and an ability to take "pleasure into being in deep s***." It's standard stuff for Bond, but it's reassuring to know Villeneuve has such a solid grasp of the fundamentals. Beyond that, the director described someone "strong, muscular, someone that is a force," as well as an individual with a "deep intelligence in the eyes" and who is "always ahead of us." Sounds about right to me. Thankfully, Robert Pattinson can fulfill every one of these requirements, which makes him one of the most exciting of all the James Bond actors.

Industry observers note that thus far, Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with positivity, even while there's been the predictable objections regarding his "Twilight" years and physicality. At this point, however, the British star has long since proved his ability to deliver consistently electric performances that always surprise. There's no reason to think his Bond portrayal will be any different. Heck, Villeneuve was convinced, and he clearly seems to know what he's talking about.

Industry News: Rings of Power Episode 6 Ending Explained: Amazon Radically Changes the One Ring's Origin Story

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 opened with a frightening scene in which Sauron (Charlie Vickers) forges a magical ring.
  • Sauron has spent much of this season trying to uncover a secret he believes Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) took to his grave.
  • This story contains spoilers for The Rings of Power season 3, episodes 5 and 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 opened with a frightening scene in which Sauron (Charlie Vickers) forges a magical ring. It was a deliberate fakeout (the Orc he tested it on burst into flames) but also a chilling reminder of the inevitable. Sauron is eventually going to forge the One Ring and come into his full power as the Dark Lord of Mordor. But he can’t seem to get it right — yet.

Sauron has spent much of this season trying to uncover a secret he believes Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) took to his grave. Episodes 5 and 6, released Wednesday on Prime Video, finally bring the missing pieces together and point toward an origin for the One Ring that diverges significantly from J.R.R. Tolkien’s canon. Here’s what The Rings of Power season 3, episode 6’s ending reveals about Sauron’s proposal, and how it changes the One Ring’s canonical creation.

This story contains spoilers for The Rings of Power season 3, episodes 5 and 6.

It has been revealed that earlier this season, the Orc Marnukh (Adam Young) led Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) and Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) to the fortress of Gundabad looking for the last of the elven smiths, mainly because Marnukh had exposed Sauron’s initiative to forge the One Ring. Sauron believed the smith knew some secret of the craft that would allow him to finally achieve it. That smith, however, had died by the time Galadriel or Sauron arrived. Galadriel’s long-lost husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) had spent years in a nearby cell. Did the smith reveal any secrets while Celeborn was imprisoned? That’s a question Sauron is willing to bet on — and torture for.

In a recent development, after Galadriel and Celeborn escaped Gundabad at the end of episode 4, they get some time alone together as they run from Sauron’s forces. In a moment of desperation as episode 5 wraps up, Celeborn surrenders himself to protect Galadriel. Unfortunately, it seems like it’s Celeborn he wants anyway. Sauron resorts to all manner of torture to get the information out of Celeborn. The worst of it is a mechanism that presses down on Celeborn’s entire body as the Orcs keep piling on more weight.​​​​​​​ For a while, it seems like Celeborn doesn’t know anything and might wind up dead.

Meanwhile, Galadriel encounters Theo, who’s spent much of this season as one of Sauron’s Nazgnagôl but is having second thoughts. With Galadriel’s help, he’s able to remove his ring. They then travel together in the hopes of rescuing Celeborn and destroying Theo’s ring.

Toward the very end of episode 6, we see an Orc head roll into view just outside of Celeborn’s new cell, and Galadriel rushes in to save her husband. A bit delirious, he proudly claims he didn’t reveal any of the secrets he knows to Sauron, specifically about the dagger that Galadriel inherited from her dead brother, Finrod. “Gold and silver from Valinor is the key,” he claims. Back in season 1, Celebrimbor melted down the dagger — which was forged in Valinor — as the raw material for the three Elven Rings​​​​​​​.

Galadriel kisses Celeborn, but as the camera pans, she becomes Sauron. All that torture was just the warm-up, and this bit of shapeshifting trickery finally gets Sauron the information he needs​​​​​​​.

In a recent development, sauron swiftly realizes that the hammer he took from Celebrimbor also contains gold and silver from Valinor, so he’s already got the raw material he needs to forge the One Ring. But there’s a problem: The hammer was forged by Fëanor, the legendary Elven craftsman who used it to create the Silmarils. (Those three jewels preserved the light of the Two Trees of Valinor, and the struggle over their possession drives much of Tolkien’s The Silmarillion.).

It has been revealed that celebrimbor’s apparition tells Sauron that​​​​​​​ no forge can melt the hammer, and even dragon fire would not stain it. The episode’s closing moments suggest the obvious answer as Mount Doom rumbles in the distance. Seemingly the only way to melt the hammer is in the fires of Mount Doom, which itself is remarked to be a sort of wound in the world created by the first Dark Lord.

Sources indicate that it now makes a lot more sense why Sauron keeps Celebrimbor’s body in Sauron’s throne room​​​​​​​ and why the dead elf seems to be haunting the newly introduced Dark Lord. Celebrimbor is, in fact, Fëanor’s only grandchild, which explains why he too was a renowned smith who had the hammer in his possession to begin with.

Sources indicate that fëanor certainly used some kind of hammer when crafting the Silmarils, but this specific tool is a novel invention unique to Rings of Power. Tolkien largely leaves the finer details of the One Ring’s creation a mystery. We know that Sauron poured a great deal of his essence into the creation of the One Ring using dark magic, and that he did it within the Crack of Doom, a volcanic fissure deep within Mount Doom. Tolkien never bothers to explain the raw materials or any other specific details.

According to recent reports, rings of Power has also made many changes to the order of events​​​​​​​. In Tolkien’s chronology, Sauron forges the One Ring around the year 1600 of the Second Age. When he puts it on, the Elves perceive his deception and remove their rings. The destruction of Eregion and Celebrimbor’s death happen in 1697, almost a century later. Once Sauron takes the Nine Rings, he distributes them to kings of Men who are gradually corrupted into full-on Nazgûl over the course of several centuries. The first recorded sighting of a Ringwraith wasn’t until 2251. Like the hammer, the Nazgnagôl Ring-servants are unique to The Rings of Power.​​​​​​​.

According to recent reports, in the show, Sauron is still struggling to make the One Ring five years after Celebrimbor’s death and the fall of Eregion. These changes also set up a bitter parallel with season 1. Galadriel surrendered her brother’s dagger so Celebrimbor could make something that might preserve the Elves’ future in Middle-earth. Sauron is now poised to destroy another cherished Elven heirloom to bring Middle-earth under his control.
