📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Recent findings suggest that any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

Sources indicate that in the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to recent reports, according to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

According to recent reports, the AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

  • Sony has released one last firmware update to ensure that it can slow down internet pirates and delay attempts at jailbreaking the PS5 post-launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 is the most anticipated release of the past decade, and Sony has been using it as its trump card to encourage players to keep their consoles up to date. If they don't update their console to the latest firmware version, the game simply won't run. GTA 6 is now within our grasp — just a few hours away from release — but gamers won't be able to jump in at launch unless they update their consoles right now.

Sony has been heavily targeted by hackers in the past few months due to the rise in piracy on PlayStation 5 systems. As more and more players jailbreak their consoles, the tech giant has been pushing PS5 updates left and right in an attempt to fight this. However, not long after an update goes live, hackers are usually able to modify their software to work around it and release it to the public again rather promptly.

Sony has released one last firmware update to ensure that it can slow down internet pirates and delay attempts at jailbreaking the PS5 post-launch. The short and vague patch notes make it clear that this is the update's purpose: "We’ve made some security fixes to the system software.".

Recent findings suggest that on X, the official PlayStation support account reminded players that they should download the update as soon as possible if they'd like to play at midnight. It's not a threat, really, but gamers won't be able to launch Grand Theft Auto 6 unless they update their PlayStation 5 to system software version 26.07-14.23.00. It requires a download of around 1.267 GB, so it's best to get to it right away. ​​​.

Rockstar has already sold millions of copies of Grand Theft Auto 6, but many more sales are almost guaranteed on launch day, so it's important for Sony to ensure that the game is protected from hackers. This is a multimillion-dollar release, and if homebrew developers are able to gain access, they might just be able to put it up on the internet for free. Many would surely be interested, especially considering GTA 6 is not going to be released on PC right away.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that feeling that chill in the air, the rising number of Oscars-hopeful movie releases in theaters, and the unmistakable threat promise of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas is You" playing in every department store you enter for the foreseeable future? Yep, you know what that means: The holiday season is officially upon us and we're positively giddy with Yuletide cheer. Of course, we're even more excited about finally having an excuse to pop on our favorite films and celebrate the festivities properly.

Recent findings suggest that for those of us who practically grew up on one particular classic, that involves ringing in the holidays with "A Christmas Story," arguably the most quintessential Christmas movie of them all. There are approximately a hundred different reasons why this of all movies captures the essence of the season the most — or, more accurately, the childlike wonder and innocence we all used to have come November of every single year. The seemingly endless wait for school to end and the fun to begin. The breathless anticipation every time our parents left the house for some clandestine gift shopping. The snowball fights and snow days and warm evenings by the fire, for those of us fortunate enough to live in more wintry climates.

In a recent development, "A Christmas Story" takes all those evocative feelings and wraps them inside a snow globe of nostalgia ... with a little commentary on crass commercialism, nuclear family dynamics, and some good ol' fashioned childhood bullying thrown in for good measure. Forty three years later, it's a pop-culture staple that endures. And one particular quote about a certain Red Ryder BB gun goes a long way towards explaining why.

"You'll shoot your eye out." — Ralph's mother.

Ah, the life-and-death stakes of being a child during the holidays. Every single item on our list is a must-have present or the world will end forever. Each day is fraught with the most impossible homework assignments we need to finish before we can have fun with friends. And every impulsive misstep or moment of misbehavior comes with the possibility of turning Santa Claus himself against us. For Ralphie (Peter Billingsley), the precocious 9-year-old boy living in 1940s Indiana retelling the events of "A Christmas Story" to us as an adult (narrated by Jean Shepherd), it all comes down to those five crushing words that destroy all his holiday hopes in one fell swoop.

According to recent reports, "You'll shoot your eye out," of course, refers to his mother's (Melinda Dillon) appalled reaction to the #1 item on his Christmas list: an Official Red Ryder Carbine-Action 200-Shot Range Model Air Rifle with a compass in the stock and a sundial, to put it plainly. It's his white whale, the forbidden fruit that torments and dazzles poor Ralphie for the entirety of the film's runtime. And when he finally works up the nerve to ask his mom for her blessing, well, she sensibly points out exactly what could go wrong with such a violent "toy.".

In a recent development, it's a perfect encapsulation of the beating heart of "A Christmas Story" and why multiple generations have gravitated towards this movie. It brings us right back to that indescribable feeling of being eight or nine or 10, with an entire world of possibility ahead ... if only the adults would let us free. After countless re-watches, well, the hilarious (and predictable) punchline proves kids don't always know best, after all.

‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A grimmer, gloomier “Hunger Games” is on the horizon with “Sunrise on the Reaping,” adapted from Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel about the origin story of the hardened alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy.
  • Industry observers note that franchise fans might be riveted by Francis Lawrence’s latest installment — points for consistency, as he’s directed all the films dating back to 2013’s “Catching Fire” — but those audiences not already invested in the dystopian material and tales of tributes will find themselves left out in the cold by an overlong (it’s 158 minutes, so get comfortable), visually soupy, and narratively morose reprisal.
  • It has been revealed that the film is set during the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A grimmer, gloomier “Hunger Games” is on the horizon with “Sunrise on the Reaping,” adapted from Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel about the origin story of the hardened alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy. Here, the teenage version of Woody Harrelson’s character in the original films is played by Australian actor Joseph Zada, the blond, ringletted Adonis who also starred as the moody Cal Trask in the recent “East of Eden” series.

Industry observers note that franchise fans might be riveted by Francis Lawrence’s latest installment — points for consistency, as he’s directed all the films dating back to 2013’s “Catching Fire” — but those audiences not already invested in the dystopian material and tales of tributes will find themselves left out in the cold by an overlong (it’s 158 minutes, so get comfortable), visually soupy, and narratively morose reprisal. But no matter, as this fresh slice of bankable I.P. is likely to rake in a hysterical amount of money, and perhaps launch Zada’s career as a face of new Hollywood stardom. Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball.

It has been revealed that the film is set during the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. Only 16 years old, Haymitch is thrust into games that are rigged from the start — and whose broadcasting is ultimately edited and deepfaked to look like pro-Capitol propaganda. (The film nudges a little bit toward the ethics of state surveillance and how footage can be manipulated or even fabricated for political ends.) His pastoral, if impoverished, life in District 12 is small but happy, with girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) and a mother and younger brother (Kara Tointon and Smylie Bradwell) with whom he shares close affinity, plus a best friend we’ll eventually find out will become the father of Katniss Everdeen (Lawrence) in the later films.

After a reaping (refresher: that’s when tributes are selected ceremonial-style, here as by a grotesquely pulled-tight-in-the-face Glenn Close as Drusilla Sickle) turns bloody, long-shot Haymitch ends up being selected at only 16. Violence follows him everywhere, as during the subsequent Tribute Parade, tragedy strikes Haymitch’s childhood friend (Molly McCann) during a horse-drawn Tribute chariot ride. Sequences meant to be thrilling often lack connective tissue to the rest of the material, or are devised in such a maelstrom of CGI (as goopy and cacophonous as a Marvel battle) that it’s difficult to feel engaged. It’s also unhelpful that most of the supporting cast is so wildly over the top, especially Capitol residents played by Close and a smarmy and mannered Kieran Culkin. Jesse Plemons as a Hunger Games camera operator brings a shade of moral dimension to the proceedings, but as with his “Digger” role, the actor feels woefully underused. Ralph Fiennes as Capitol president Snow, meanwhile, is given but scraps of material to work with.

According to recent reports, the by-the-book script by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie appears to stick faithfully to Collins’ 2025 novel, with plenty of potential for visual appeal that goes largely unrealized. The Hunger Games arena Haymitch is thrust into is rife with hidden dangers: poisonous streams, a deadly force field, and other trippy flora and fauna that vibe like a dark mirror version of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” but again, “Sunrise on the Reaping” trips up on the CGI fakery.

Sources indicate that the movie’s stacked young cast of tributes and mentors (those victors of previous Hunger Games tournaments) includes Mckenna Grace as a District 12 tribute who’s not to be trusted, the endearingly wily Ben Wang (recently excellent in the SXSW film “Brian”), plus a gravely underused Maya Hawke as the winner of the 49th Hunger Games, Kelvin Harrison Jr. as victor of the 34th, and the great Lili Taylor as a legacy tribute played previously by Lynn Cohen (aka Magda on “Sex and the City”) in the second film. These characters mostly exist to introduce themselves to Haymitch, be established as good or evil or helpful or unhelpful, and then be shuffled out of the scene. Elle Fanning is rather amusing, however, as the Capitol stylist Effie Trinket, styled and nearly drowned out by extremely outré fashions. Glenn Close also (with a visage channeling Katherine Helmond as Ida Lowry in “Brazil”) could’ve been used to better effect.

In a recent development, the specter of death looming over the film should not be confused for much in the way of actual depth, and while Zada’s performance is charming enough, his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films. He feels like a cog or a function to get this prequel to line up with the prior films — and isn’t that what he is? Which makes the movie, and ergo probably the book, feel a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series’ lore. When Haymitch comes home from Second Quarter Quell and descends into depression and alcoholism, that’s when the movie gets most interesting. Not a great sign when your film’s tepid coda is also its best moment.

Recent findings suggest that and equally worrying is a series of cameos tacked onto the film’s end that smack of depressing fan service. These movies seem to be mostly critic-proof and hugely appealing to their core audience, but “Sunrise on the Reaping” is a dreary slog, another death-march “They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?” riff with a pretty Gen Z cast, and one that mistakes upcoming layers of darkness (and trauma!) for the sort of profundity that its filmmakers hope will burnish a creatively withering property.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters on Friday, November 20.

Amazon's Jeff Bezos Clarifies Involvement In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As exciting as it is that Robert Pattinson has been cast as James Bond, the irony of his 007 movie being overseen by a man who is about as close to a real-life Bond villain as you're likely to get is inescapable.
  • Industry observers note that bezos appeared at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event where he confirmed that he was "heavily involved" in Pattinson's casting (via Twitter/X).
  • .@JeffBezos tells @lizrhoffman he was "heavily involved" in selecting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As exciting as it is that Robert Pattinson has been cast as James Bond, the irony of his 007 movie being overseen by a man who is about as close to a real-life Bond villain as you're likely to get is inescapable. What does Amazon founder and chairman Jeff Bezos know about movies? Well, that remains unclear. But since Amazon bought Bond for an eye-watering sum back in 2025, he is the man who cuts the checks at the end of the day. That means he was always going to have a say in who plays Bond and it seems he was, indeed, intimately involved.

Industry observers note that bezos appeared at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event where he confirmed that he was "heavily involved" in Pattinson's casting (via Twitter/X). "We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on [the Friday before the official announcement was made the following Monday]," he stated. "There was a substantial group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists.".

.@JeffBezos tells @lizrhoffman he was "heavily involved" in selecting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Sources indicate that "Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he's already so famous ... but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond." pic.twitter.com/1ro4R8meYO.

— Semafor (@semafor) November 17, 2026.

According to the Amazon founder, the process of whittling down the finalists (let's agree never to use the phrase "down-selected" again) involved carrying out "old-fashioned screen tests" which he described as "interesting." These tests apparently involved "full costumes and real sets and other actors," with Bezos going on to explain how each of the five candidates performed three scenes on-camera. "Then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that," he continued. "By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance. It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director ... we all gravitated toward Rob.".

It has been revealed that it's interesting to hear Jeff Bezos' recollection of how Robert Pattinson was cast as James Bond. Soon after Amazon made the official announcement, reports emerged that claimed Pattinson wasn't actually director Denis Villeneuve's first choice for Bond. Instead, it seems the director was set on casting "Wake Up Dead Man" and "Disclosure Day" star Josh O'Connor, before the actor chose to take himself out of the process. To hear Bezos tell it, however, all five Bond finalists screen tested and the clear favorite was Pattinson.

Those finalists reportedly comprised O'Connor, Pattinson, "Slow Horses" star Jack Lowden, Callum Turner of the "Fantastic Beasts" films, and the man who will seemingly forever come in second to Pattinson: Nicholas Hoult. Rather than Pattinson being a second choice, in Bezos' recollection he simply came out on top after the screen tests and the decision was about as close to unanimous as you can get.

Recent findings suggest that with all that in mind, it remains unclear just how the final days of the casting process unfolded. Was O'Connor still in the running on that Friday Bezos and co. watched the screen tests? How late, exactly, did Pattinson enter the process, considering he reportedly had to escape his "The Batman: Part III" contract ahead of his Bond casting? What is clear at this point is that the Amazon founder was right there alongside producers and Villeneuve to oversee the final decision.

In a recent development, interestingly enough, during his Semafor event comments Jeff Bezos also claimed that Robert Pattinson didn't start out as the favorite for "Bond 26." "Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he's already so famous," he noted. "Like, maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.".

In a recent development, indeed, Pattinson's 007 casting breaks a 60-year tradition of casting relative unknowns as the legendary spy. As such, you can appreciate why the producers were hesitant at first. Ever since "Dr. No" introduced cinema's most enduring franchise back in 1962, audiences have gotten used to seeing a fresh face in the role with each latest recasting. But Pattinson's star power is actually one of the reasons he could be the best Bond yet. The last few entries in the franchise haven't been the most impressive, and the "Primetime" star will surely help restore a sense of prestige to a saga that's felt quite stale for some time. That's to say nothing of his considerable acting talent, which will no doubt immediately convince the naysayers the moment they see any footage from the film.

According to recent reports, that certainly seems to have been the case with Bezos and the gang, who evidently felt Pattinson was a cut above the other Bond hopefuls after seeing his screen test. It remains to be seen what sort of influence the Amazon founder will have over Denis Villeneuve's movie during production, but let's hope he's too distracted by world domination to interfere too much.

#27892. The GTA 6 Review

The GTA 6 Review

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Who gets to break the rules in America?
  • It has been revealed that when we first meet the co-star of Grand Theft Auto 6, she’s scraping the bottom of the cultural barrel.
  • When Lucia is finally set free, it’s not because society has decided that this financially desperate Latina has earned a second chance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Who gets to break the rules in America? A cryptobro living off of financial scams. A girlboss CEO who turns feminine vulnerability into a pyramid scheme. A cop who shoots a civilian in the face and walks away scot-free. It’s an exclusive club of societally acceptable grifters and killers, and Lucia Caminos’ name isn’t on the VIP list.

It has been revealed that when we first meet the co-star of Grand Theft Auto 6, she’s scraping the bottom of the cultural barrel. She’s a lowly street rat. The only person who seems to give a damn about her is Jason Duval, another small-time crook who connects with her during a star-crossed carjacking turned meet-cute. It doesn’t take long for the law to interrupt her rom-com dreams, landing her in prison with other low-tier riffraff crammed together like sheep in a pen.

When Lucia is finally set free, it’s not because society has decided that this financially desperate Latina has earned a second chance. It’s because of an overcrowding crisis at the jail.

Sources indicate that in a sprawling satirical sandbox filled with loudmouth radio DJs and over-the-top conservative cartoons, it’s the sharpest stab GTA 6 lands on American culture. Justice is massive business in the Florida-inspired state of Leonida, and people like Lucia are products to be cycled in and out of a flawed system. All the while, the real criminal masterminds of Leonida trash their penthouses into the wee morning hours.

It has been revealed that lucia’s unjust origin story is the key to understanding and embracing GTA 6’s tantalizing power fantasy, panicked parents and politicians be damned. Rockstar Games’ astonishing open-world adventure, the most impossibly grand and expensive video game that may ever exist, doesn’t just generate its morbid pleasure from cop-killing sprees and armed robberies; that comes from living in a reactive place governed by intricate rules that beg to be bent and busted. If you can learn to outmaneuver police helicopters and escape with duffel bags full of unmarked bills, you’ll be rewarded with a small taste of the law-breaking freedom that’s only offered to a certain class of crook in America.

It has been revealed that it’s no wonder that, after decades of moral panic, GTA once again earns its title as public enemy #1 — only this time, Rockstar accomplishes that less through bloodshed and more with an empathetic love story built for an era of stark economic uncertainty. It’s a bold choice, considering the series’ cold-blooded reputation, but it’s also what makes GTA 6 one of Rockstar’s finest games to date.

In a recent development, following an opening prologue that ends with Lucia behind bars, the story really kicks off as her sentence is winding down. Jason, now living in a dilapidated shack in the Keys, has found a modest living doing odd jobs for Brian, an old-timer who has mastered the art of laying low far outside of Vice City. When Jason receives word that Lucia is getting an early release, it lights a fire under him to get his house in order so that the lovers can have a chance at a normal life. Key word: normal.

The opening chapter, filled with low-level crimes and mundane roof-patching missions, makes for a strong introduction to a story about a couple scraping by. Whereas some GTA games explicitly focus on the myth of the American Dream, following wannabe kingpins who can’t get enough money and power, Jason and Lucia’s motivations are more down to Earth. The duo’s ultimate goal is to earn enough cash to skip town and support one another. While you can spend your riches on guns and designer clothing, your substantial-picture aim is to fill up a savings account via the in-game BuckMe cash app. That’s the real dream.

It’s a more human GTA story that’s sold by Jason and Lucia. Both characters get equal screen time during the campaign, and both are compelling leads in their own way. Jason is a veteran, a detail that’s never deeply explored, but one that subtly establishes him as a person who has been left behind. Why is he living in a leaking shack and reduced to working shady gigs while patriotic right-wing media dominates Leonida’s radio waves and TV stations? There’s a lingering sense that he’s been used and tossed aside on the literal outskirts of America.

In a recent development, jason is also a true himbo: a monotone musclehead who reveals his heart of gold early on when quietly obsessing over home renovation tasks once he learns Lucia is getting out. He has the energy of a young Channing Tatum, with charm and sincerity always poking through his tough guy persona. Jason also works as the perfect straight man for the oddball rat race that is Leonida. He’s just as confused as you are when a stranger escapes a car crash and decides to hop back into the burning vehicle to ensure he gets a bigger insurance payout. The shit people will do for money in this town.

But Lucia is the real star of the power couple. She’s unapologetically brash, and has no reservations about getting back to a life of crime after getting out of prison. That can make her seem one-dimensional at first, but it’s grounded in a real anxiety that crops up between her snarkiest one-liners. A key flashback shows her struggling to make ends meet as a ride-share driver, weathering racist abuse from passengers who in turn tank her rating. There’s a sense that she’s hit a dead end in a world that hates her; even an app is rigged against her. She sees little choice but to accept risky jobs in hope that she can put even $500 into her bank account. The shit this town makes us do for money.

Leonida is full of natural predators that circle its swamps like hungry alligators.

The central story, which has the rhythm of a five-season prestige TV series, sees the couple graduating to bigger crimes and even bigger apartments as they move throughout the state. Small gigs in the Keys soon give way to harmless carjackings upstate, and then to tense bank robberies in Vice City’s urban core. While there are some thrilling heists along the way that require meticulous planning across multiple missions, the story can sag when it’s inventing elaborate excuses to tutorialize features, reposition Jason and Lucia around the map, and introduce last-minute villains in time for its rushed final stretch. Instead, its most effective moments come in all the quiet conversations that happen between bank jobs, where Jason and Lucia trade insecurities about the viability of their shared future in a place like Leonida.

In a recent development, that feeling does not exist in a cultural vacuum. In true South Park fashion, Rockstar takes as many potshots as it can at the current state of American culture. It plays out like a damning, if sometimes dated, retrospective of the past decade — you could subtitle it “I Hate the 2020s.” Jason finds himself tangled up in a crypto scam. Lucia stumbles into a multi-level marketing scheme disguised as a noble women’s wellness business. Flip on a radio, and you might catch the all-too familiar sounds of a conservative whining about trans athletes in school sports, only to reveal that he’s a little too eager to "protect" young girls, if you catch my drift. Leonida is full of natural predators that circle its swamps like hungry alligators.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the environment that our antiheroes find themselves sinking in while the bastards swim. Petty theft will earn someone like Lucia an immediate trip to jail, but everyone else appears to be getting away with much worse. Through its satirical mirror, GTA 6 questions why some people need to play by the rules while others don’t. (You can even see that reflected in the game’s own comedic targets: Rockstar goes out of its way to avoid lampooning powerful political figures like Donald Trump, but it’s not shy about dunking on rural rednecks and people living in the slums, struggling with substance use disorders.).

It has been revealed that it doesn’t always feel like there’s much an individual can do to topple structural inequities in real life. But in a safe digital playground like this? You can start to understand the inherent appeal of blowing off steam in GTA 6’s punching-bag world.

Sources indicate that while there’s a lot to unpack in this downright enormous game, the basic catharsis of GTA remains unchanged here. When you’re not working through story missions filled with third-person shootouts and car chases pulled straight from a Hollywood movie, you’re free to cause as much chaos as you want in Leonida. Jack a car, mug a pedestrian at gunpoint, rob a gas station — live your criminal fantasies as long as you can before the police rain on your parade. Decades after it first stirred moral panic, GTA’s appeal remains its unmatched ability to let players see just how much they can get away with as you test your relationship to authority.

Video games are a perfect avenue for that because they’re built on rules. You can only jump this high. You can’t access this area until you’ve found the right key. Killing this character will result in this consequence. Every time you enter a latest world, your immediate task is to learn the law of the land. Your second, and more fun, task becomes figuring out how and when to break those laws. GTA 6’s greatest strength is that it offers an entire nation of laws. They spill out from countless criss-crossing systems that require you to keep your head on a swivel at all times.

Industry observers note that steal a car without scanning it first with a phone app that reveals its security system, and you might find yourself panicking when an unseen tracker starts beeping. Fail to find someone hiding in a back room during an attempted bank heist? They’ll have enough time to get free and trigger an alarm. Robberies are an especially strong addition to GTA 6 in that respect — not just because they let you explore interior spaces, but because they require you to get every detail right. You need to act quickly to compel guards to drop their guns, threaten cashiers to hand over safe codes, or destroy any security camera footage hiding in a server room. There are so many ways you can screw up unexpectedly, but that makes it all the more satisfying when you pull off a clean getaway just before the cops pull up to the scene of the crime.

Even GTA’s signature wanted system requires much more of your attention now, as police are now able to track your car, face, and outfit if someone sees you. Listen to the cops on your scanner, and you’ll hear them sharing the vehicle and outfit you were spotted in, or even your build. You’re not even fully out of the woods when you outrun the fuzz, as you’ll leave a temporary heat level in the area you committed a crime as cops continue to look for you. My first three-star chase was a 30-minute cat-and-mouse game that had me abandoning vehicles and scrambling over fences to get away. Just when I thought I was safe after having thrown on a hat and glasses, the chase began again once a passing cop car got a look at me for a moment too long.

In a recent development, all of this is different for a GTA game that is chasing a certain level of hyperrealism. Here, Rockstar very much builds on the groundwork it laid in 2018’s laborious Red Dead Redemption 2. For instance, you can build muscle by following a strict workout routine that requires you to do a certain number of reps within a set time period, and even build rests into your training regiment. If you want to steal a locked car without smashing the window and setting off an alarm, you’ll need to use a slim jim to carefully pick the lock. While that attention to detail could often feel tiresome in the slow-paced world of Red Dead, everything moves mercifully faster here, which makes sense considering that you’re barreling around town in sports cars instead of plodding down dusty roads on horseback.

Still, it takes some adjusting to. In my first sessions, I found myself almost scared to do anything I wouldn’t do in real life. Something about the photorealistic visuals has changed my usual GTA brain chemistry; I was suddenly stopping at traffic lights and refusing to cut in front of cars. But that would end up being a functional anxiety. Every session offered another opportunity to see what rules I could bend. Broken traffic laws led to quiet stick-ups in isolated pawn shops led to full-scale assaults on Leonida’s most well-guarded banks. Progression like this is baked into a story of escalating crimes, but it’s also built into the very psychology of GTA 6.

It has been revealed that it’s easy to get reductive when discussing the broad appeal of GTA. Many would have you believe that its popularity is a symptom of a sick society that glorifies crime and violence. Maybe there’s some truth to that, but it doesn’t get to the heart of the series. Its joy has more in common with a kid screwing around in class as much as they can without landing in detention. When you possess little power in the world, there’s a pleasure in getting to push what buttons you can. (Even calling out sick from work to play GTA 6 on launch day can be seen as workers exercising the tiniest bit of institutional rebellion.) That’s made all the more powerful in this story, with these characters, within this laundry list of intricate laws.

None of this would matter much if the world wasn’t worth living in, but Leonida makes for the perfect setting. An enormous map that has been in the works since 2015, as Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson told Polygon in an interview last week, GTA 6’s take on Florida packs an entire state’s worth of scenic landscapes and local eccentrics into one coherent place. While returning players might be most excited to spend time in the glitzy Vice City, that’s arguably the least interesting location in the game.

In the south, you have the Leonida Keys. Almost designed with the same tutorial zone philosophy underpinning Breath of the Wild’s Great Plateau, it perfectly captures the compact, distant nature of the real Florida Keys. It feels like you’re in a world physically detached from the state, where you don’t have a lot of avenues for escape if you go on a murder spree. It’s the perfect place to learn the rules of the road before things open up the further north you get. That stands in contrast to the very top of the state, a wide open rural landscape that’s built for hunters and hikers (and, unlike IRL Florida, actually features topography of differing elevations). Some of my favorite moments of the game so far have simply come from biking around mountains and stumbling into off-road racetracks and crumbling ruins.

It’s the rare open-world game that feels a mile wide and a mile deep.

It has been revealed that there’s a lot to take in, especially considering how much work Rockstar puts into locking down the right aesthetics. The world itself is astoundingly detailed, with everything from a crowded strip club to a stray island off in the water feeling like it was hand designed and placed with purpose. That comes at the expense of peak performance, as GTA 6 runs at 30 frames per second with some dips when police chases hit the five-star mark. But that’s a negligible impact on the overall experience, given how smoothly it runs most of the time. (I played GTA 6 on a PS5 Pro.) And it’s a fair trade for a world that deserves its own line of postcards.

It has been revealed that driving around it is an auditory delight too, as GTA 6 features a soundtrack so large and diverse that you have to wonder if half of the budget went to music licensing. Metallica and Slayer are there for the metalheads, Charli XCX and Chappell Roan for the modern pop aficionados, and a whole lot of Trick Daddy and Juvenile for those who want to pay respects to the greats of the Dirty South rap scene. All of is spread between satirical commercials and radio shows that clue you into Leonida’s political climate as you drive. (Though be prepared to hear a lot of low-hanging dick jokes; GTA 6’s writers lean hard on cocks as a comedic crutch.) Every little artistic touch helps bring Leonida to life beyond its landmarks.

While there’s plenty to see and hear, I’m more impressed with how much of the world doesn’t feel constructed for players to explore. I occasionally drive by the kind of roadside construction areas that you pass by while on the highway. I don’t think much of them in real life; that’s not an area that I need to pull over and see! GTA 6 mirrors that experience, loading the world with so many mundane sights that ground the world in realism. You can go to them, of course. You might even find a collectible trading card or a wad of cash there. But there’s always a sense that life is happening in Leonida, even when you’re not there.

The best example is in how Jason and Lucia stumble into happenings in Leonida. While the map is filled with markers indicating main story quests, robbery locations, and other activities of note, many other things can just happen out of nowhere. Entire side quests can be discovered by noticing a guy drunkenly barreling down the highway on a tractor, or following the voice of a man looking for his lost cow. Those missable moments often hide the best quests in GTA 6 and imbue the world with more personality than you can imagine.

According to recent reports, other world events aren’t there to kick off missions at all. In one session, I heard the sound of police sirens and followed them downside road to find the cops surrounding a garage. A woman emerged and revealed that she was making kitty litter in there, not drugs. That wasn’t tied to a quest, nor did it have any story implications or rewards tied to it. It’s just a thing that I happened to catch. I’ve similarly seen plane crashes in the distance, watched the cops get into a standoff with a furry, and passed under a bridge as a group of troublemakers above threw tires down on the cars below. Sometimes I insert myself into those situations. (I sure gave those rabble-rousers a talking-to.) Other times, I decide it’s just not my business. The fact that I can make that choice adds a remarkable level of depth to Leonida, a place where you’re always reminded that Jason and Lucia aren’t the only two people who are up to some shit. Everyone is off on their own hustle.

That barely begins to cover what you can experience in Leonida. There are shooting ranges, golf courses, basketball hoops, meditation spots, diving expeditions, stunt jumps, drone-flying challenges, scannable landmarks, and more collectibles than you can imagine. Hell, there are multiple street racing leagues that will make you feel like you’re playing Forza Horizon 6 as streets get repurposed into natural circuits. There’s even an extensive vehicle modification system to allow you to fine-tune cars to your liking. It’s the rare open-world game that feels a mile wide and a mile deep.

Recent findings suggest that what’s surprising about all of that is that it somehow avoids feeling totally overwhelming. Maybe it’s just because there’s so much to do that it’s easy to accept from the jump that you will likely never see it all, but I haven’t felt a compulsion to do anything in GTA 6. Everything is just another potential avenue to make money in a world where stable employment isn’t an option for Jason and Lucia. Want to earn a living fencing cars? You could just do that. Feel like busting up meth labs and selling the goods instead? You’ll have plenty of opportunities. The ultimate power of GTA 6 is that you have the freedom to pick your poison and carve out your own life in Leonida. Why shouldn’t Lucia have that privilege that’s afforded to everyone around her?

Sources indicate that so, you can break all the rules in GTA 6. You can do more crimes than ever before. You can kill seabirds and throw them at people. You can amass a fortune on mounds of stolen cocaine and unmarked bills. So what?

That’s an key question not just for finding value in a video game that you could probably play for a decade, but in real life too. One of my deepest daily anxieties comes when I think too hard about existing in an employment battle royale. I know that I need a job to get the money to live, but what’s the point? Aren’t I just busting my ass for the privilege of waking up another day and busting my ass again? I spiral over it constantly; the eat-work-sleep cycle becomes claustrophobic the more I focus so tightly on it that I can no longer see its endpoint. (I imagine that Rockstar’s own staff may be grappling with similar feelings right now, as they are at the moment fighting to unionize.) It’s easy to lose your hope, motivation, or sense of self when you don’t have something to fight for.

Sources indicate that GTA 6’s secret weapon for addressing that malaise comes back to Jason and Lucia. A video game starring a couple has a lot of upsides on a pure design level, and Rockstar takes full advantage of that dynamic. You can freely swap between characters outside of some early story stretches, allowing you to dress up and manage two heroes with distinct personalities. Some missions even have you flipping between them during dramatic set pieces, letting you cover yourself when you wind up pinned down during a tense shootout. When you’re about to do a bank robbery, you can invite your partner to the spot and go in together to ensure you can carry more bags and cover your vulnerabilities. When you leave, you can even command one character to head off and fence the spoils instead of lugging it back to a buyer manually. All of these scenarios allow you to think more strategically about how you pull off crimes, and how you spend your time.

According to recent reports, but what’s more effective is how the two can interact when they’re not on the job. GTA 6’s real hero feature is an optional relationship system that allows you to create a romantic bond between Jason and Lucia. When I’m playing as one character, for instance, I can pull out my phone and call or text my partner. (You can text and drive, but be prepared to learn why you should never do that in real life.) That can be just to check in and see how they’re doing, or to invite them to come hang out on a whim. They’ll arrive either in their own car or a ride-share a few moments later, and you’ll find yourself on an impromptu date.

In a recent development, the benefits of GTA 6’s activity-filled world and systems-heavy design reveal themselves in those tender moments. One time, I took Lucia out for a round of mini-golf. Another time, I invited her out to the club and spent hundreds of dollars on champagne for us as we danced together. At any point, you can pull up a menu that allows you to strike up a conversation, flirt, or even hold hands. The two can also fall into natural conversations while hanging out. One time while driving, a country song came on the radio. Lucia started talking about how she thought country music was a big joke growing up, prompting a sweet little exchange between the couple as they chatted about the genre. It felt like a real conversation that would come up with your partner during a road trip.

In a recent development, I already know the wild story moments that GTA 6 will be widely remembered for — there are some fantastic ones involving a pulse-pounding airport caper and an accidental porn set misadventure. But I don’t think I’ll remember many of the repetitive drive-and-shoot chases that clog up a long story that recycles the same ideas a few too many times. Instead, it’s the intimate interactions that stick with me now. One of my favorite moments in the entire game didn’t happen during a mission or cutscene at all. It was when I woke up one morning to find Lucia standing on the balcony of our apartment. I walked up behind her, gave her a kiss, and held her in silence as we looked out across the beach below. I let it play out as long as I could before heading out for another day of blood and bullets.

That’s the so what. Through Jason and Lucia’s genuine chemistry, GTA 6 gives you a better reason to work through Leonida’s daily grind. Yes, there’s always another bank to rob or car to steal, but that’s not the reason you wake up in the morning. It’s to prove that love can survive in a cruel culture that tries so hard to beat it out of people. So be it if you have to play dirty to keep pace with the cold-hearted crooks who make their fortune from someone else’s pain. It shouldn’t be this hard to settle down with your lover and enjoy a sunset together in the rotten social climate that Rockstar has been eager to lampoon for decades at this point.

People will hem and haw about Grand Theft Auto’s purported glamorization of lawlessness. They always have; they always will. But it will be different this time. GTA 6’s empathy is bound to be the most controversial thing about it.

Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. The game was reviewed on PlayStation 5 Pro using a prerelease download code provided by Rockstar Games. You can find additional information about Polygon’s ethics policy here.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

10 Years Ago Today: Hailee Steinfeld Starred In One Of The Best Coming-Of-Age Movies Of All Time

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Actor Hailee Steinfeld broke out in the Coen Brothers' 2010 Western film "True Grit" as the precocious Mattie Ross, who speaks like she's wise beyond her years but lacks the experience that brings true wisdom.
  • Sources indicate that nominated for an Academy Award at only 14 years old, it would've been easy for Steinfeld's career to have peaked there.
  • It has been revealed that after a premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, "The Edge of Seventeen" hit theaters on November 18, 2016.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Actor Hailee Steinfeld broke out in the Coen Brothers' 2010 Western film "True Grit" as the precocious Mattie Ross, who speaks like she's wise beyond her years but lacks the experience that brings true wisdom. We at /Film consider Steinfeld as Mattie the greatest performance in any Coens movie, which is no small feat.

Sources indicate that nominated for an Academy Award at only 14 years old, it would've been easy for Steinfeld's career to have peaked there. But she has kept challenging herself with music, voice acting, and plenty of new movies, and one of her best is absolutely writer/director Kelly Fremon Craig's coming-of-age film "The Edge of Seventeen.".

It has been revealed that after a premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, "The Edge of Seventeen" hit theaters on November 18, 2016. It takes its title from the Stevie Nicks song yet applies it more literally to this story about a 17-year-old girl. The acerbic, awkward, and unpopular Nadine Franklin (Steinfeld) has lost the two people in the world who understand her. One, her father, Tom (Eric Keenleyside), who died a few years prior of a heart attack. Now, her best friend, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has started dating Nadine's older brother Darian (Blake Jenner), whom Nadine loathes for having their mother Mona's (Kyra Sedgewick) favor and being so effortlessly beloved and successful.

"I've gotta spend the rest of my life with myself," Nadine says while drunk. We all realize that and then come to terms with it at some point. Nadine's story fits in the gap between the realization and the coming to terms. Speaking as someone who was the same age as Nadine was in 2016, and saw "The Edge of Seventeen" in his senior year of high school, few coming-of-age movies depict awkward adolescence in the 2010s more honestly.

Critics compared "The Edge of Seventeen" to a modern John Hughes movie, as did Hailee Steinfeld herself. In 2016, she explained to Entertainment Weekly that she hoped that the movie could reflect her generation's teen years back at them while still being timeless, in the same way "Sixteen Candles" and "The Breakfast Club" — films made for 1980s kids — still resonated with her (someone born in 1996).

Industry observers note that but "The Edge of Seventeen" doesn't soften itself by looking to echoes of older movies instead of real life. The film begins with Nadine marching up to her history teacher, Mr. Bruner (Woody Harrelson) in his classroom, announcing she's planning to die by suicide and wants someone to know first. That opening makes you think you're in for a movie about an inspirational teacher who talks a depressed student back from the edge and indicates them why life is worth living. Well, not quite.

According to recent reports, we see, as Mr. Bruner immediately recognizes, this is Nadine being dramatic. "I don't want to take up a ton of your time" she notes right off, which is her first lie. The movie then rewinds (with the help of some voiceover from Nadine, though that fades pretty rapidly) before catching back up with this cold open. What led to her current situation? Nadine accidentally sent a text to her crush, Nick (Alexander Calvert), describing very explicitly how she wants to hook up with him.

Sources indicate that that complements one of the best bits of writing in the film, one that definitely helped it speak to my younger self. Nadine has a lot of movie-typical teenage boy qualities: she doesn't fit in, dresses in baggy sweatshirts, has a hopeless crush she never talks to, makes sex jokes while mistaking vulgarity for wit, etc.

During the "Edge of Seventeen" press tour, Kelly Fremon Craig and producer James L. Brooks spoke with /Film. Craig cited some "life-altering" writing advice from Brooks, that she needed to ask herself, "What is this movie saying about life?" I would answer that "The Edge of Seventeen" is about how, when you're a teenager, your problems seem like the whole world and that part of growing up is realizing others — even people who irritate you everyday (as Nadine's mom and brother do to her) — are dealing with their own pain.

Sources indicate that upon its release, "The Edge of Seventeen" saw only modest financial success, grossing $19 million in theaters against its $9 million budget. A spin-off TV series ordered by YouTube Red ultimately didn't move forward, either. I would also argue the film's anticipated reputation as "definitive teen movie of the 2010s" was overshadowed by Greta Gerwig's "Lady Bird," which came out the following year and hits similar beats while finding both great financial success and critical acclaim. Not that "The Edge of Seventeen" has been lost to time or anything, though.

According to recent reports, in that aforementioned /Film interview, Craig claimed, "If [Hailee Steinfeld] didn't exist, the movie wouldn't exist," because she brought a sui generis quality to Nadine as she once did to Mattie Ross. The two would work together again on the "Transformers" spin-off film "Bumblebee," where Steinfeld starred and Craig performed rewrites. "Bumblebee" often feels like "The Edge of Seventeen" but with Transformers included.

Industry observers note that A couple of times in "The Edge of Seventeen," Nadine looks up to the sky and asks if God is even paying attention to her. Perhaps it's not surprising that when Craig directed another coming-of-age film, she adapted Judy Blume's classic novel "Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret.".

#27889. Industry News: Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1232 w)

Industry News: Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people.
  • According to recent reports, but a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films.
  • According to recent reports, this alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people. Born in the twentieth century at the wrong place and time? Beware of Nazis, AIDS, and other mortal dangers. Hollywood has at times depicted these threats in ways that emphasize the humanity of LGBTQ+ people, as when Tom Hanks played a lawyer dying of AIDS in “Philadelphia,” during the height of the epidemic in 1993. The industry also has a history of finding ever more creative ways to kill off and scapegoat queer characters, a trope that as recently as 10 years ago seemed to be running amok.

According to recent reports, but a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films. After years of what felt like permanent advances in rights and representation, LGBTQ+ people have been stung by backlash, including attacks on gender-affirming care, legal threats to marriage equality, and cuts to suicide prevention. Amid a reduced perception of safety, anxieties about the possibilities and consequences of nonnormative desire are spilling out onscreen like so much fake blood. Even so, their formulation is evidence of social and creative progress. Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball.

According to recent reports, this alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films. In Adrian Chiarella’s “Leviticus” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” same-sex attraction engenders extreme and potentially deadly terror, be it from detractors or the people it consumes. Both films explore not the evils of queerness — an argument that belongs to the tradition of queer-coded villains — but the horrors of having one’s desires villainized.

In a recent development, the year’s queer history films also subvert conventional narratives around sexuality and deadly fates. In Andrew Scott’s awards-season vehicle “Elsinore,” Ian Charleson’s dying wish to play Hamlet is one many actors would share; the film doesn’t focus on how or why he has AIDS, but what he wants to do before it kills him. The Spanish epic “La Bola Negra” depicts forbidden romance, but desire isn’t what dooms its multiple generations of queer men. The fact that they’re swept up in the currents of history, just like everyone else, is part of the film’s revolutionary power.

The era for combatting the notion that being gay is a no good, very bad thing in a straightforward way finally seems to have passed. Usually such sermons were preaching to the choir anyway. Gone is the teary earnestness of a conversion therapy drama like “Boy Erased,” from 2018, in which much of the trauma wrought on Lucas Hedges’ character derives from the church but is carried out by earthly messengers. In “Leviticus,” when a healer tries to pray the gay away from a pair of lovesick adolescents, he conjures supernatural and murderous doppelgangers.

After rituals of deliverance are performed over the convulsing bodies of a pair of schoolmates (played by Joe Bird and Stacy Clausen), each one is haunted by an illusion of the other that tries to kill them. The concept of “Leviticus,” named for the Old Testament book that forbids man to lie with man, partly functions as a wry play on the idea that you never get over your first crush. It also takes the fear that so many queer people know well — that what you desire most will be your downfall — to literal and horrifying extremes. Imagining the bigotry of organized religion as a senselessly violent supernatural force is a radical reversal. The boys aren’t the problem; the boogeymen that torment them spring from the so-called good book.

Sources indicate that schoenbrun’s meta queer fantasia “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” likewise performs a canonical revision. The nonbinary killer in the campy franchise within the film were themselves killed and sunk to the bottom of a lake by their comically gender-panicked peers. A victim seeking revenge, the TV-headed slasher is called Little Death, a nod to a French term for orgasm, la petite mort. Hannah Einbinder’s millennial filmmaker is on a quest to reboot the franchise, but more significantly, to achieve her own “little death.” In order to grow more comfortable with sex, and give into her own desires, her fear of intimacy — one that, again, many queer people know well — needs to be killed.

According to recent reports, the movie ultimately intertwines fear of death with the fear of intimacy in a way that demonstrates the stakes — how you can feel so afraid of getting close to someone you could just die. But what must be slaughtered in this case is fear itself — so that same-sex desire, which has so often been pathologized and villainized, can flourish. (The trail of straight people extravagantly dispatched along the way, like so many gays before them, is one of the film’s many deranged and delightful flourishes.).

There is a potent realignment evident in the year’s period films as well, which center the desires and fates of queer characters on their own terms, rather than taking their oppression or disease as subjects unto themselves. “Elsinore” leans a bit heavily on obvious sentiment while leaving much of the thematic richness of “Hamlet” on the table. But Charleson’s determination to play the part before he dies is what drives the film, while the indignities of succumbing to AIDS are mostly a secondary plot.

Contrast that with recent period dramas on TV, like “It’s a Sin” (2021) about young people facing the AIDS crisis in London, or “Fellow Travelers” (2023) about the Lavender Scare in the U.S., and focusing on Charleson’s dream itself rather than the injustice of what threatens it marks a distinct shift.

Recent findings suggest that the broad sweep of the canvas in “La Bola Negra” heralds another major turn of the page. The play of the same name by Federico García Lorca that partly inspires the movie, and appears in one of its several timelines, is about a young man denied access to an elite social club because he’s presumed to be gay. But homophobia isn’t the primary struggle (or a harbinger of death) for the film’s other gay characters. It certainly doesn’t help two doe-eyed young men (played by Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente) brought together and kept apart by the Spanish Civil War. But the forbiddenness of their infatuation is just one current swirling around them, the most pressing of which is, well, the Spanish Civil War.

According to recent reports, weaving the fates of queer characters into the broader scope of history, and suggesting a lineage of ancestry and shared desire, as “La Bola Negra” so marvelously does, feels like a kind of imaginative reparations. And it marks a bolder, more robust tactic in humanizing queer lives; the film traces generational ties and uncovers untold histories, rather than contending with acute crises like religious doctrine or deadly disease.

Industry observers note that there is a stranger and more expansive creative palette evidenced in these films, one that suggests the unnerving climate for queer people in the real world is only furthering the reaches of the imagination. In carrying forward the legacy of queer cinema, it seems the gays presumed buried by the trope are finally rising up.

The Rings Of Power Season 3's Best Storyline Redeems A Controversial Peter Jackson Idea

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching Season 3, Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.".
  • Recent findings suggest that over halfway into its run, it's clear "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 is spectacular whenever Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is on-screen.
  • But it's not all doom and gloom, as Season 3 also introduces the brightest light of hope in Middle-earth: the elven golden retriver Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching Season 3, Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.".

Recent findings suggest that over halfway into its run, it's clear "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 is spectacular whenever Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is on-screen. Indeed, this season is for the baddies, with the Dark Lord's menacing Nazgnagôl making their grand entrance and a thrilling civil war brewing in Númenor.

But it's not all doom and gloom, as Season 3 also introduces the brightest light of hope in Middle-earth: the elven golden retriver Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). From the moment he indicates up, it feels like he's been a part of the show from the start, fitting in perfectly as a strong, funny, flirty elf who has excellent chemistry with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark). Celeborn is the ultimate wife guy, and his relationship with Galadriel is the best romance we've seen in a Middle-earth adventure to date.

In a recent development, nevertheless, there's trouble in Valinor for these two, as Celeborn has competition for Galadriel's heart. No, not Robert Aramayo's Elrond (despite them sharing a kiss in Season 2 to distract the orcs holding Galadriel captive), but Sauron, the Dark Lord on his dark throne in the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.

According to recent reports, that's right: "The Rings of Power" Season 3 has finally turned "The Lord of the Rings" into a romantasy story, placing a love triangle at the heart of the saga of the One Ring. And while J.R.R. Tolkien purists may scoff at this, the show's love triangle is so good that it redeems the controversial romances from Peter Jackson's otherwise beloved "Lord of the Rings" films.

Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films are the most widely celebrated fantasy movies of all time and changed the genre forever. As such, it's easy nowadays to forget that Jackson's trilogy stirred up its fair share of controversy upon its initial release. After all, as faithful as they were to J.R.R. Tolkien's original books overall, those films also made some big alterations. That includes erasing the Scouring of The Shire from "The Return of the King" and removing characters like Tom Bombadil and Glorfindel, in addition to introducing a prominent love triangle.

In Jackson's movies, to jog your memory, a respectable amount of time is spent on Éowyn (Miranda Otto) falling in love with Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), with even King Théoden (Bernard Hill) buying into their match and congratulating Éowyn on finding a good and honest man. Meanwhile, Aragorn keeps thinking about Arwen (Liv Tyler), who is about to leave Middle-earth for Valinor. In fact, the original proposal was for Arwen to be at Helm's Deep alongside Éowyn and Aragorn in "The Two Towers," which presumably would've fueled their love triangle even further.

Industry observers note that things get even worse in Jackson's "The Hobbit" films. There, he and co-writers Philippa Boyens and Fran Walsh introduce Tauriel (Evangeline Lilly), an elf who develops romantic feelings for the dwarf Kili (Aidan Turner). In that case, it's Legolas (Orlando Bloom) who rounds out the love triangle, as he's still racist towards dwarves at the time.

Neither of these Middle-earth love triangles really work (especially not the latter), so it's hard not to be skeptical of "The Rings of Power" introducing yet another one. And yet, this ends up being the most compelling aspect of Season 3.

There are two things that make the love triangle in "The Rings of Power" work. The first is that the show is very clearly in on the joke, with Sauron often behaving like a teenager when it comes to his borderline hilarious fixation on Galadriel. That he even goes to the trouble of disguising himself as Galadriel and kissing Celeborn to get information out of him indicates Sauron is not beyond being a little bi-curious.

In a recent development, then there's the fact that the series has been building to this since Season 1, starting with Galadriel slowly falling for Sauron in disguise as Halbrand and being seduced by his promises of power. By the time Season 3 rolls along, she still has complicated feelings for him, as evidenced by her dreams and visions of Sauron waking up in bed next to her. Thus, when Celeborn re-enters her life, and Galadriel sees both men in front of her, there's a tiny bit of hesitation on her part.

Recent findings suggest that and yet, Season 3 never suggests that Galadriel would actually leave her husband for the Dark Lord. Instead, it juxtaposes Sauron's jealousy with Celeborn's confidence. Specifically, in Episodes 5 and 6, Sauron gets visibly flustered when Celeborn talks about how much Galadriel loves him. In the end, it works just as well as the incredible romances in J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, proving that Middle-earth is not devoid of effective romantic storytelling.

Heck, the scene in Episode 6where Celeborn talks about making the elven smith that Sauron has been looking for tell him the secrets of the rings, just so he can hear about every minute the smith spent with Galadriel, is arguably the most romantic TV scene of 2026. Stream Season 3 on Prime Video, and see for yourself.

  • The pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months.
  • In a recent development, at long last, things are finally changing.
  • Industry observers note that audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Movie theater owners have been through hell.

The pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months. When they could finally turn their marquees back on, Omicron and other variants made audiences skittish about returning to cinemas. Then the writers’ and actors’ strikes upended production, leaving them with fewer movies to screen. A promised moviegoing revival kept getting delayed or disrupted, often by circumstances outside of the exhibition industry’s control.

In a recent development, at long last, things are finally changing. Domestic ticket sales are up 20 percent year over year, and with potential blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three,” “Avengers: Doomsday,” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the horizon, analysts expect revenues to easily eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID. Grosses in North America presently sit at $8.76 billion through November 15, fueled by franchise fare such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5,” but also by unconventional hits ranging from “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to “Obsession” and “You Can See Everything.” Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team.

Industry observers note that audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon. And media companies, which treated the theatrical business as the sick man of the entertainment industry, are finally seeing the value in cinemas, with the likes of Amazon MGM Studios and Skydance committing to making more movies for the major screen than most major studios did over the last decade. Better yet, younger viewers are driving the comeback, with studies showing that Gen Z members are the most frequent moviegoers.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the good news. Elsewhere, Hollywood seems to be crumbling. Netflix, which has done more to reshape the entertainment industry this century than arguably any other tech giant, is teetering, having jettisoned both chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin in a brutal purge. Ted Sarandos, who is clearly feeling the heat after the company’s stock has fallen 35.6 percent year-to-date, has brought in Peter Rice, a well-regarded former Fox and Disney exec whose calm demeanor and unthreatening good looks are out of c-suite central casting, to steady the ship.

It has been revealed that as Hollywood has stumbled around trying to develop a better business model, the solution that many companies have landed on is to get bigger, fast. Thus, Fox sold to Disney, MGM was auctioned off to Amazon, and David Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount and then quickly merged it with Warner Bros. Others, such as Comcast, spun off assets to make themselves more digestible. Has it worked? That’s the $80 billion question at Skydance, where executives have pledged to make 30 movies a year and turn a combined Paramount+ and HBOMax into a true Netflix challenger. Yet Ellison must pull this off while paying down a massive amount of debt.

Sources indicate that so far, their early moves haven’t inspired much confidence. Executives like CBS News chief Bari Weiss have embraced the Silicon Valley ethos of “move fast and break things,” but what they’ve built instead, such as a simulacrum of “60 Minutes,” doesn’t seem better than what they’ve replaced. And if, as a recent Variety story about Skydance’s post-merger strategy suggests, part of their cost savings involves making sure executives don’t send out for “sandwiches and green juices” from Erewhon, they’re in for a world of pain. They can have Jimmy John’s cater lunch, and it won’t make a dent in their debt.

Skydance has already laid off most of Warners’ leadership and offered buyouts to the rank-and-file. Another wave of layoffs is expected at the company any day now. And across town, those types of cuts are the default move, with everyone from Disney and NBCUniversal to Amazon and Sony slashing hundreds of jobs. Are some of these layoffs in anticipation of what a leaner, AI-assisted future might bring? Probably. But with many of these companies’ share prices flatlining or falling, they aren’t being enacted out of foresight or a position of strength.

“I can’t remember a time when things have felt so scary,” an entertainment executive confessed to me recently.

Recent findings suggest that and they’re right. It’s always popular to say the movie business is dying or the television industry is collapsing, and those doomsayers have been proven wrong time and time again. People want to be entertained. It’s just that making money entertaining them has never been harder for Hollywood.

U.S.-based players will have to be careful to avoid spoilers for essentially the whole day on Wednesday.

Maybe you can't wait to play GTA 6 when it launches in your time zone and want to get your hands on it early. I get it. Tech Report: 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible.
  • In a recent development, if you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule.
  • Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

In a recent development, if you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Recent findings suggest that variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Recent findings suggest that waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze claims it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most crucial to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

According to recent reports, waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

It has been revealed that if you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

If you don't want Waze storing certain types of data—or if you want to keep your activity hidden from other owners—you can adjust various privacy settings in the app. You will certainly want to turn off personalized ads (under Settings > Privacy) and consider enabling invisible mode, which keeps your username, mood, photo, and online status hidden from other Waze users. Finally, you can delete recent locations and drives as well as your navigation history at any time.
