Meta's VR Glasses Could Be The Future Of Home Viewing (But They Probably Won't)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in stark contrast to the dire straits that the movie theater industry was in just a few years ago, 2026 has been especially encouraging to those of us who adore going to the movies.
  • As usual, however, the tech industry isn't far behind to try and stoke the competition between theaters and home viewing.
  • Recent findings suggest that I recently had the opportunity to try these glasses for myself, and their potential, especially for home viewing, is amazing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in stark contrast to the dire straits that the movie theater industry was in just a few years ago, 2026 has been especially encouraging to those of us who adore going to the movies. A big part of why that's changed lies in the industry's embrace of unique Premium Large Formats, with numerous releases this year having been shown in formats like IMAX, 4DX, Screen X, Dolby Cinema, and so on. Along the way, screening on celluloid (70mm in particular) have become a draw unto themselves, and some cities are home to even more specialized formats, among them Las Vegas' immersive Sphere and the Cosm experience. And while the biggest draw to movie theaters will always be good films, it's clear that audiences also enjoy an experience they can't get elsewhere.

As usual, however, the tech industry isn't far behind to try and stoke the competition between theaters and home viewing. While most consumers have been content with things like big screen 4K TV's or even their handheld devices for watching at home or on the go, the latest attempt to leap forward from these is just around the corner, in the form of Meta's VR Glasses. It's crucial to note that these are not the latest version of the smart glasses that have existed on the market since 2021, as they're explicitly not designed to be used while engaged in other activity. Instead, they're a cutting edge virtual/augmented reality system intended to bring together multiple work and entertainment options while idle.

Recent findings suggest that I recently had the opportunity to try these glasses for myself, and their potential, especially for home viewing, is amazing. That said, there are some restrictions to them which, unless changed, mean they won't be replacing our existing personal devices anytime soon.

Although virtual reality, or VR, has existed in some form for decades, it's mostly been utilized as a gimmick more than a viable first choice for media. Fortunately, the folks behind Meta VR Glasses seem to understand this. I got to see a clip from the recent concert doc "Billie Eilish — Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour (Live in 3D)" on the glasses, and the experience was like I was watching it on a movie theater screen. That is to say that the aspect ratio was exactly the same as its theatrical exhibition, and the 3D display was pitch perfect. Turning my head in any direction didn't move the "screen," but kept it fixed in front of me, as if it was a physical object in the space, which is a very smart design.

While the James Cameron documentary acted as a demo of how watching most films and shows on the glasses would go, the Meta employees next indicated me what they're calling "Enhanced Cinema." Using a clip from "Avengers: Infinity War" in which Thor (Chris Hemsworth) constructs Stormbreaker, the presentation was almost exactly akin to the Cosm experience. This meant that the film was playing on a similar fixed "display" in front of me, while all around me (literally 360 degrees — I checked!) was the environment of the forge on Nidavellir. It's an effect that's totally immersive but not distracting, nor does it betray the original intent of the film itself. After being told that Meta has an exclusive license with the IMAX corporation to present movies filmed for that format on the glasses, I have no doubt that the device could brilliantly replicate those screens for home viewing, and that's incredibly exciting.

While the Meta VR Glasses are not intended to replace a smartphone or similar device, they do seem to do a lot of what those devices do, only bigger and better. From working on VR video games and multiple computer monitors at once to allowing you to watch sports games as they broadcast while seeing the view from courtside, the glasses seem almost too good to be true as a personal media device.

Recent findings suggest that this is where the catches come in. For one thing, watching something with other people at the same time can only occur depending on the content. For another, though they're engineered to be used while stationary, the temptation for people to wear them in public while walking (or, god forbid, driving) exists, and it's quite troubling. Then there's the fact that the glasses seem designed to only work with whatever services and content Meta allows. This means that us physical media fans are SOL, and as with any all-digital service, the content available on the glasses could be subject to change (or disappear) at any time. That's a lot to ask for a device priced at $1,299.99 USD, which is about the same as a fresh iPhone.

Right now, Meta's killer app beyond the tech itself are its exclusive licenses, such as with IMAX and James Cameron's Lightstorm Entertainment. The only way it'll compete with devices already on the market is if it can consistently deliver the quality experiences I got to have with it while being as user friendly as possible. If the glasses prove they can be used at home and on the go as smoothly as an iPhone can now, then they could be a game changer. Until then, they're just a gimmick, albeit a really nice one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that dividend stocks remain a popular choice for investors seeking steady income and higher portfolio returns. However, with thousands of dividend-paying companies to choose from, identifying the right stocks can be challenging.

In this regard, recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can provide useful insights and help identify dividend stocks backed by solid fundamentals and with attractive upside potential.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Sources indicate that independent oil and natural gas firm Permian Resources (PR) is this week's first dividend stock. The company recently paid a quarterly base cash dividend of 16 cents per share. At an annualized dividend of 64 cents per share, PR offers a dividend yield of 3.5%.

Recently, Evercore analyst Chris Baker initiated coverage of Permian Resources stock with a price target of $25. The analyst believes that the manufacturer is well positioned to benefit from improving U.S. shale demand after the Iran conflict, thanks to its low-breakeven inventory that can boost free cash flow growth. Baker also noted PR's disciplined consolidation in the Permian Basin.

In a recent development, furthermore, the 5-star analyst highlighted the company's focus on a single basin and management's efficient capital allocations across expansion efforts, strategic acquisitions, and share buybacks. Baker noted that management focuses investments on the higher-return Northern Delaware Basin, helping boost profitability.

"The key piece of our work here, and the reason we think PR deserves a higher multiple relative to more finite or less flexible shale stories, is that PR runs an acquire and exploit model," mentioned Baker.

The 8 Best Fantasy Book Authors of All Time, Ranked

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that fantasy has been present in stories for just about as long as human storytelling has been a thing, but it didn't become an actual marketing label for the publishing industry until around the 19th century.
  • Sources indicate that but even though there have been hundreds upon hundreds of great fantasy writers over the years, there are eight in particular who can be considered the very best to ever grace the genre.
  • After graduating with a Bachelor's degree in Philosophy from the University of Manitoba, Canadian author Guy Gavriel Kay began writing poetry before turning to prose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fantasy has been present in stories for just about as long as human storytelling has been a thing, but it didn't become an actual marketing label for the publishing industry until around the 19th century. Since then, we have gotten thousands of authors who can be called full-on fantasy authors, and there is many an element that makes up a great one. Without boundless imagination, deep technical craft, a purposeful eye for world-building, and the ability to write grounded characters, no fantasy author can be truly great.

Sources indicate that but even though there have been hundreds upon hundreds of great fantasy writers over the years, there are eight in particular who can be considered the very best to ever grace the genre. These are authors who aren't just phenomenal from a technical or artistic standpoint, they are also of vital historical importance to the genre, still influencing countless fantasy authors the world over to this day. Their work is as foundational as it is essential, and their names belong on the bookshelf of all fantasy fans.

After graduating with a Bachelor's degree in Philosophy from the University of Manitoba, Canadian author Guy Gavriel Kay began writing poetry before turning to prose. Soon enough, he became one of the greatest—and most underrated—fantasy authors of his generation, penning many forgotten books that have aged like fine wine. His work has been particularly key in revolutionizing the mixture between fantasy and settings strongly resembling real historical places and periods, even though Kay himself rejects the label of historical fantasy.

Kay was hired by Christopher Tolkien to help assemble and edit J. R. R. Tolkien's chaotic mass of posthumous manuscripts into the legendary The Silmarillion.

Recent findings suggest that before he published a single novel of his own, Kay was hired by Christopher Tolkien to help assemble and edit J. R. R. Tolkien's chaotic mass of posthumous manuscripts into the legendary The Silmarillion, and that alone should already be proof enough of his quality. After that, he became a true pioneer of inserting historical elements into the high fantasy genre, delivering masterpieces of the caliber of Tigana and The Lions of Al-Rassan.

Robin Hobb is the pen name of Margaret Astrid Lindholm Ogden, who's undoubtedly best known for her iconic Realm of the Elderlings megaseries. It wasn't until she turned 30 that she published her first book under the name of Megan Lindholm, proving that it's never too late to join the pantheon of history's greatest fantasy authors. She began writing as Robin Hobb 12 years later, and her debut under that legendary pen name was Assassin's Apprentice, the first book in the Farseer trilogy from the Realm of the Elderings series.

Exploring themes like otherness, gender, and queerness across her incredible work, Hobb has crafted some of the fantasy books with the best world-building and the best character writing in history. Shifting the genre's focus from earth-shattering spectacle to deep psychological intimacy and philosophical complexity, she proved just how character- and theme-driven the genre could be when written by a gifted enough author.

If there's any one author worthy of being called the most prolific and widely celebrated fantasy writer presently working, it's almost undeniably Brandon Sanderson. His debut novel, Elantris, was published in 2005, by the time Sanderson had already written about a dozen unpublished books. He has been nothing but a writing machine since then, best known for his iconic Cosmere universe. Composed of multiple subseries and standalones, it's one of the best ongoing fantasy book series.

According to recent reports, from the Mistborn series to the Stormlight Archive, Sanderson has written several of the most ambitious high fantasy books of all time, all the while building the biggest multi-decade meta-narrative that fantasy literature has thus far seen. Off the page, he has also trained and influenced countless authors over the years, and coined the distinction between hard magic and soft magic systems, being the undisputed master of the former.

British author, literary scholar, and Anglican lay theologian C. S. Lewis also wrote some incredible science fiction, but he's obviously better known for his fantasy work, particularly The Chronicles of Narnia, one of those fantasy series where every book's a masterpiece. He began writing fiction as a child, inventing stories with his brother and fellow author, Warren Lewis; and soon enough became one of the most notable English writers of his generation.

Sources indicate that alongside his good friend Tolkien, Lewis still stands as one of the major pillars of modern fantasy. His work not only revolutionized and popularized portal fantasy, it also made fantasy as a whole more widely accessible, more culturally ubiquitous, and more deeply rooted in Western mythology and philosophy than ever before. Without authors like him, who's to say whether fantasy would have ever been fully legitimized as a genre worthy of being taken seriously?

Sources indicate that another instance of a fantasy literature legend who's best known for one particular series, but whose contributions to the genre extend far beyond that, Robert Jordan is the must-read author of some of the most perfectly-written fantasy books in history. He decided that he wanted to write books while recovering from his time as a Vietnam War veteran, and began writing while working as a nuclear engineer for the US Navy.

High fantasy had been very heavily inspired by Tolkien (or directly aiming to imitate him) for decades before Jordan came about.

In a recent development, the most prominent work of such an iconic career is The Stormlight Archive, far and away one of the greatest and most influential fantasy book series since the '90s. High fantasy had been very heavily inspired by Tolkien (or directly aiming to imitate him) for decades before Jordan came about, and it was authors like him who proved that the genre could start doing things differently. Darker, more mature, and more complex than most other fantasy novels from his time, Jordan's work broke the mold and has continued aging like fine wine.

According to recent reports, dramatic fantasy is of vital importance, and it's always a delight to read an author who actually takes the genre seriously and builds something deeply compelling out of it. However, comedic fantasy is arguably every bit as notable, and as far as that subgenre goes, you don't get any authors more foundational than Sir Terry Pratchett, fantasy's most beloved satirist. He's best known for his Discworld series, composed of a whopping 41 fantasy comedies.

Recent findings suggest that what makes Pratchett's work so brilliant is that even though his satirical fantasy works are undeniably hilarious, they're also surprisingly profound. On top of providing one of the best soft magic systems in history, Discworld proved that even comedic fantasy could be legitimately serious in its own way. Thematically complex and richly human, Pratchett's work interrogates human nature, institutions, and morality in all sorts of enrapturing ways. His books are brilliantly meta and quite diverse, making Discworld a must-read series for anyone who thinks that fantasy can't be hilarious and profound at the same time.

Sources indicate that in the entire history of speculative fiction, few authors have ever been quite as important as Ursula K. Le Guin. Indeed, the American master could also very reasonably be counted among the eight most important and essential sci-fi authors of all time, but there are many who prefer her work in fantasy. Le Guin wrote her first fantasy story at age nine and submitted her first sci-fi story to a magazine at age 11, and from there, there was nowhere for her to go but up.

In a recent development, the daughter of an anthropologist and with a deep academic interest in mythology, Le Guin wrote masterpieces like Lavinia and the Earthsea Cycle, many of them among those books that are a masterclass in high fantasy writing. By introducing elements of Taoist philosophy, psychological realism, and non-Eurocentric anthropological and cultural depth to her work, Le Guin completely rejected many of the tropes and traditions that had ruled fantasy literature for years. She genuinely revolutionized fantasy, pioneering many newly introduced tropes of her own in the process.

You'd be hard-pressed to find anyone unwilling to call J. R. R. Tolkien the single greatest and most influential fantasy author of modern times, and that's for good reason. Never has the history of speculative fiction seen anybody quite like Tolkien, and it likely never will again. Sparked by the Professor's love for philology, ancient mythologies, and original myth-making, the world was treated to an authorial career that completely revolutionized fantasy. Indeed, many would divide the genre's modern history between the pre-Tolkien and the post-Tolkien eras.

According to recent reports, yes, Tolkien wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, his most celebrated works and perhaps the most influential fantasy novels of the 20th century. However, his contributions to the genre extend far beyond. He wrote several masterworks outside Middle-earth, he contributed to the academic study of fantasy, and he completely laid down the blueprint for modern high, epic, and heroic fantasies. Author of some of the most memorable characters, the most fascinating lore, and the best battles in the history of fantasy books, Tolkien was the greatest of all fantasy writers. It will take someone so special that he's truly out of this world to ever dethrone Tolkien.

Industry observers note that four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

Industry observers note that you want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

According to recent reports, you would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

According to recent reports, as part of the moves, Jesse Ehrman has been promoted to president of Warner Bros. Pictures, while Mikey Ireland will remain as president of production. Their task will be to stabilize Warner Bros.‘ film output while rejuvenating or extending franchises like “The Lord of the Rings” and “The Conjuring.” Skydance executives have been horrified by the extent of the losses racked up by Pam Abdy and Michael De Luca, with sources estimating them in the hundreds of millions of dollars. As part of this restructuring, Jeff Goldstein, who oversaw Warner Bros. distribution for many years, will retire, and Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, which he led. Skydance remarked that in the interim, Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee all animation across both Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures. Richard Brener, a survivor of several mergers, will remain as president and chief content officer of Fresh Line, where he guided hits like “Weapons.”.

Others remaining include: Lia Buman, EVP, head of global acquisitions and Republic Pictures; J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, heads of the genre division, Paramount Primal; and Christian Parkes, head of the indie label Clockwork; and Charlie Tabesh, SVP and general manager of Turner Classic Movies.

Last week, Skydance announced that James Gunn and Peter Safran, who had led DC Studios, were leaving the company. Jeremy Latcham, a former Marvel executive, replaced them. It wasn’t the only overhaul at the top. Last month, as Skydance took full control of Warner Bros., Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy were ousted. De Luca and Abdy were beloved by the creative community, but they spent liberally and accumulated too many flops, including “Digger” and “The Bride!”.

According to recent reports, both Granger and Goldberg will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, the co-chairs of Skydance’s Motion Picture Group. Across Paramount and Warner Bros., the mandate will be to get more films into production. To get the merger over the finish line, Skydance founder David Ellison agreed to make more than 30 films annually, far exceeding the output of any traditional studio.

Recent findings suggest that in a memo to staff, Goldberg and Greenstein praised Granger as “a great partner as we’ve repositioned the studio, bringing in key talent relationships and nearly doubling output.” They noted that at Netflix, Goldberg “oversaw a slate that included ‘Don’t Look Up,’ starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, and the upcoming ‘Bad Day,’ with Cameron Diaz, and ‘The Take’ starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Goldberg was also an executive at Fox, working on films such as “The Greatest Showman” and “Bohemian Rhapsody.”.

“Together, Don and Kira will work hand in hand going forward,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote, adding, “We have both an incredible legacy to build upon and an enormous opportunity ahead of us: to champion the world’s best filmmakers, invest in ambitious storytelling and deliver an unparalleled slate of films that captivate audiences everywhere.”.

Ehrman is a WB veteran who has worked on hits such as “A Minecraft Movie” and “Sinners.” Ireland joined Warner Bros. after years at Paramount. He left the studio after it was sold to Skydance in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that “This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote. “We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gabriel Luna has a rule: He doesn't play villains unless it's opposite "the greatest action hero who's ever lived," aka Arnold Schwarzenegger.
  • Recent findings suggest that this isn't just an aspirational goal.
  • In a recent development, luna plays Ray Ballard, aka the Sleepy-Eyed Killer, across two episodes of Dexter: Resurrection season 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gabriel Luna has a rule: He doesn't play villains unless it's opposite "the greatest action hero who's ever lived," aka Arnold Schwarzenegger. "I have an I only play heroes kind of mindset," the actor tells Polygon.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't just an aspirational goal. It's already happened twice. Luna portrayed Rev-9, an advanced killer robot in Terminator: Dark Fate, and he was an evil arms dealer in the Netflix series FUBAR, both of which starred Schwarzenegger. But in 2026, Luna broke his own rule to take on a very different kind of role: a serial killer.

In a recent development, luna plays Ray Ballard, aka the Sleepy-Eyed Killer, across two episodes of Dexter: Resurrection season 2. It's a role he was drawn to because of the complex psychology at work within the character, who stalks and kills his victims while they sleep.

"I was fascinated by the psychological warfare he plays with them as he does these home invasions and enters the home for weeks and weeks before he ever culminates the kill," Luna notes.

Speaking to Polygon, the Last of Us star goes deep into the backstory he invented for the Sleepy-Eyed Killer and the surprising record he broke while shooting his most pivotal scene.

Spoilers follow for Dexter: Resurrection season 2 episode 3.

Luna does have some experience with serial killers. He played real-life detective Rafael Tovar in the 2025 miniseries Devil in Disguise: John Wayne Gacy, where he helped track down the infamous murderer. Luna learned a lot about what makes someone become a serial killer while working on the show; specifically, that many serial killers tend to have experienced a childhood trauma of their own.

"Hurt people hurt people," Luna states.

The actor took that lesson and applied it to Ray Ballard as an explanation for why he kills.

Recent findings suggest that "It's mostly about freeing these people from the binds that they have to family, to other human beings in general," he indicates. "They can only serve to hurt you.".

Industry observers note that "That's something that was probably beaten into him. Some kind of heinous abuse he endured early in his life, which is often the case. This guy was definitely messed up somewhere in his childhood. The people who were closest to him abandoned and abused him. He was never able to shake that and forgive that, and now he's taken it out on everyone.".

Like so many serial killers before him, Ballard ultimately winds up on Dexter Morgan's operating table where Michael C. Hall's anti-hero delivers his own unique brand of vigilante justice by tying them down under sheets of plastic wrap, reminding them of their terrible crimes, and then murdering them in cold blood.

According to recent reports, plenty of great actors, from John Lithgow to Neil Patrick Harris, have met the same fate on Dexter. However, Luna's death scene appears to have broken a very specific record.

"I may have set a record for most time on the table, which I'm very proud of," Luna notes, citing the show's executive producer, Scott Reynolds, as his source.

Sources indicate that "That scene was a bit long. It starts with a whole scene between Michael and Uma [Thurman], and then it transitions into a scene between Michael and I. And so I spent a lot of time on the table that day. I don't know what they clocked it at, but apparently it was a record.".

You're completely strapped to the table, and they have a little sippy cup with juice for you and feed you Cheerios or whatever you wanna eat and just hand it like a baby bird.

Records aside, Luna seemingly had a blast being murdered onscreen in a scene that involves Dexter driving an ice pick (Ballard's murder weapon of choice) right into the serial killer's forehead.

"It's such an iconic place to be," Luna states. "Many greats have been on that table and have felt the point of Dexter's knife.".

According to recent reports, "You can't move, and your arms are bound to your sides. You're completely strapped to the table, and they have a little sippy cup with juice for you and feed you Cheerios or whatever you wanna eat and just hand it like a baby bird.".

That doesn't exactly sound like fun, but maybe Luna is just built different. Then again, it probably helped that his wife was also there to keep him company in between takes.

"My wife, who's a massive fan of the show and has always been, was on set that day," Luna states. "We have a great photograph of her standing over me as I'm bound, completely wrapped in Saran Wrap. I've joked that she could ask me for anything in that moment, and I would've been powerless against her.".

Dexter: Resurrection is streaming now on Paramount Plus.

Ring's Fresh $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other organization, capturing more than 40% of the market.
  • According to recent reports, the drone camera is one of two products in the organization's latest Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad.
  • The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other organization, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company confirmed a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

According to recent reports, the drone camera is one of two products in the organization's latest Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the tech giant has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

Industry observers note that but there's something slightly unsettling to me about the idea of a robot patrolling my home while I sleep. Yes, I know that there are privacy and security features in place—Ring states the videos its robots capture are protected by its "strongest default encryption yet"—but it's also yet one more example of how comfortable we've all gotten with cameras being absolutely everywhere, to the point that people think nothing of putting them all over their homes. (This is probably why I don't own a robot vacuum.) And it doesn't help that the drone sounds absolutely terrifying, which Ring claims is by design: "If someone’s there who shouldn’t be, a flying drone overhead...makes it clear they’ve been spotted. [The] devices are built to deter, not just monitor." True enough, but there's also no getting around the fact that drone propellers are unavoidably loud, and the sound of the Ring Drone Cam reminds me of nothing more than the screeching violins in a horror movie. (Note that the drone we were shown was white, but the final version sold will be dark grey.).

#27876. ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russell film, but all involved seem to want to downplay that fact.
  • Industry observers note that to be fair, this isn’t the worst promotional strategy.
  • Russell may shifted to streaming but his commitment to allowing actors to go substantial or go home remains sacrosanct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Madden” is technically a David O. Russell film, but all involved seem to want to downplay that fact. Amazon MGM Studios, in their infinite wisdom, has decided to emphasize star Nicolas Cage’s performance as the larger-than-life NFL coach and sports broadcaster in its scant promotional material. While the trailer includes an obligatory “From the director of ‘Silver Linings Playbook’ and ‘American Hustle’” title card, the poster features Cage and Christian Bale, who plays Oakland Raiders coach Al Davis, flashing their Super Bowl rings, and no mention of Russell. Even the PR flack at the sparsely-attended press screening introduced the film by saying, “Please enjoy Nicolas Cage’s ‘Madden’!” Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball.

Industry observers note that to be fair, this isn’t the worst promotional strategy. Russell may be a problematic figure, but it wasn’t so long ago when starring in one of his films almost guaranteed an actor awards attention. During a brief five-year period in the 2010s, his work garnered Oscar wins for Christian Bale and Jennifer Lawrence, and nominations for Amy Adams, Bradley Cooper, and Robert De Niro. Putting aside the uneven quality of his work, Russell certainly afforded actors the opportunity to “make choices” in lavish studio productions, which often amounted to adopting broad accents and wearing flashy costumes, and receive acclaim for their efforts. It’s probably why people keep working with him in spite of the numerous incidents of on-set mistreatment (on top of a sexual assault allegation) that have continued to this day.

Russell may shifted to streaming but his commitment to allowing actors to go substantial or go home remains sacrosanct. In “Madden,” Cage wore 30 pounds of prosthetics on top of the 25 pounds he gained for the role. He certainly resembles the man, at least if you ignore Cage’s actual face. Ditto Bale, who adopts Davis’s Noo-Yawk accent and bold fashion sense. But it’s all in service of a film so milquetoast that it will make you beg for the sheer personality exhibited in “Amsterdam,” which at least had the decency to have a narrative and occasionally spark tension and generally be about something.

Recent findings suggest that here’s what happens in Russell’s eleventh feature: head coach John Madden leads the Oakland Raiders to finally beat their longstanding rivals Pittsburgh Steelers in the 1976 AFC Championship, after which they win the Super Bowl. Following his diagnosis of a bleeding ulcer in his stomach, Madden permanently retires from his coaching career to be with his family. Realizing he’s a stranger in his own home after spending too much time away, he quickly transitions into sports broadcasting where he becomes a television mainstay. To secure his legacy and pass on his legendary playbook, he eventually lends his likeness to EA Sports for the “Madden” video game franchise, which becomes one of the most profitable on the market. He then lives happily ever after.

In a recent development, if that sounds like a film with little-to-no conflict, you would be correct. Part of the problem is that Madden, while being an American institution and a legendary NFL coach, isn’t really suited to be the subject of a biopic, largely because the details of his life are fairly free of drama or intrigue. He’s the kind of figure who should be the lead of a Saturday-morning cartoon where he helps kids solve mysteries using the power of his football mind. Rather than impose a zany plot onto his life or make up outlandish shit for entertainment purposes, which he’s known to do, Russell dutifully relates the major events in his life.

Sources indicate that the bare-bones emotional foundation of “Madden” takes the form of the two loves in the eponymous character’s life. The first is with his wife Virginia (Kathryn Hahn), who longs for John to recommit to fatherhood and their marriage, at least until it becomes clear that he needs football to be a functioning human being. Hahn’s established joie de vivre ensures Viriginia is slightly more interesting than an archetypal long-suffering wife character, but, alas, her general lack of chemistry with Cage dampens their tender scenes together, and their intermittent marital troubles are too fleeting and half-hearted to make any dramatic purchase.

The second, and arguably most pivotal, is with Davis, whose slightly-problematic bromance with Madden serves as the film’s primary source of drama. Russell’s film briefly flirts with an interesting thread by portraying Davis as a devil on Madden’s shoulder, someone who seemingly wants him to continue coaching forever, his health and family life be damned. He constantly tries to pressure Madden into returning to the league long after he retires in the vein of an old buddy who wants you to stay out for “just one more beer.” Despite his size, Madden frequently shrinks in Davis’s presence, who knows just what to say to get him to do what he wants.

But while Russell gestures towards connecting Davis’s “maverick” professional style, which made him uniquely qualified for the world of sports ownership but nevertheless created controversy within the league, and his friendship with Madden, he ultimately chickens out from characterizing him as a truly malign influence. (“Madden” just isn’t set up to be a film with a villain or an antagonist of any kind.) Instead, Russell depicts John and Virginia Madden and Al and Carol (Sienna Miller) Davis as tightknit couple friends, admittedly a type of relationship that rarely receives the big-screen treatment, whose ups and downs are manageable because, well, they really just love each other.

Recent findings suggest that it’s worth noting that “Madden” is technically a comedy. It certainly presents as one, featuring well-proven settings for laughter in sports comedies like the sidelines, the locker room, and the announcing booth. Intermittent jokes pop up in these spaces, though I’m genuinely hard-pressed to remember anything specific because much of it suffocates under Cage’s affectionately-caricatured performance. Russell trusts that the sight of the actor in a full-body fat suit is enough for audiences. Granted, Cage seems to palpably enjoy embodying Madden’s flamboyant energy and imposing figure, even if his inconsistent voice acting, complete with slurred speech and vowel-swallowing, occasionally threatens to tip into outright cruelty. (“Madden” features the real article speaking at the film’s end and it’s downright absurd how much Cage exaggerates his diction.).

It has been revealed that if there’s one semi-sophisticated bit in the film, it’s that Madden’s one-track mind sees the world entirely through football strategy. He literally can’t write “XOXO” to his future wife in their yearbook without turning it into a play design. But Russell doesn’t really develop the idea any further and instead defaults to broad humor that tends to blend together and subsequently die on the vine. These often materialize as sight gags, like Bale’s increasingly ridiculous haircuts, or John Mulaney, who plays Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins, costumed to resemble Steve Jobs. Sometimes it amounts to Shane Gillis delivering Shane Gillis-style lines, sometimes with a perm or donning a wizard’s outfit, or former running back Marshawn Lynch dressed like a nerd.

Sources indicate that on paper, Russell is actually a neat fit for a film like “Madden.” He made his bones directing abrasive ensemble screwball comedies. He’s directed period biopics, including one that’s also a sports drama, and one of his most acclaimed films involves football fandom. Sadly, “Madden” features few Russellisms beyond tacky ’70s and ’80s fashion and some mild domestic discord. He’s replaced his typically messy, chaotic atmosphere for an overly genial one.

Industry observers note that anyone who has some familiarity with screen passes or end-arounds likely learned it downwind from Madden, who used whiteboards to make complicated play schemes accessible to the viewing public. His impact extends well into the realm of pop culture, like the Miller Lite commercial where he breaks through the wall, the custom-manufactured bus in which he drove around the country due to his well-documented fear of flying, and his famous turducken. “Madden” covers all of that material without offering any insight other than the security of the man’s legacy. The Russell who made “I Heart Huckabees” has long faded away, but it’s still a shame that he’s been reduced to directing one of the oddest and blandest examples of brand management in recent memory.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “Madden” in select theaters and on Prime Video on Wednesday, November 18.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that star Wars has opened up the door to an exciting possible future for the Knights of Ren, after the Sequel Trilogy failed to fulfill their potential and then unceremoniously killed them all off in Rise of Skywalker. Those deaths are all still very much canon, but the franchise has thrown a canon curveball by revealing that those were not officially the Knights.

According to recent reports, record scratch moment. What? Then who were they? Well, the short answer is that they were the former Knights of Ren. In a latest piece of the Sequel era puzzle, Star Wars has shed more light on the Knights of Rens' fate, as an order. As it turns out, one did escape their fateful confrontation with Ben Solo and Rey Skywalker, and she is still out there waiting for the next chapter of her story to be written.

It has been revealed that as for the Knights that fell in Rise of Skywalker, they had been stripped of their titles by that point. Before breaking good, Kylo Ren declared the order all but disbanded, with only one true Knight of Ren remaining in the galaxy.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for Star Wars: Fall of Kylo Ren #4!

Recent findings suggest that star Wars fans were hyped for the Knights of Ren, latest villain Kylo Ren's personal bodyguard, when their designs were first released ahead of The Force Awakens. As the Sequel Trilogy played out, though, the Knights were reduced to barely there bit players, all but cut out of the movies. Now, the franchise has provided a self-aware reason why: the Knights of Ren were actually posers all along.

Sources indicate that star Wars has hinted at this before, but it is the point of The Fall of Kylo Ren #4, as the miniseries finds itself on the precipice of The Rise of Skywalker. In the glitch, the Knights try to get back in Kylo's good graces, conspiring to murder his rival for leadership of the group, Tava Ren. Instead, he steps back and waits to watch as she slaughters them. Only for Tava to declare that they aren't even worth the blood on her hands.

Recent findings suggest that tava spares them and takes off. After she leaves, Kylo strips the survivors of their "Ren" titles. "That's done," he says. They will still be his lackeys, and warm bodies for him to throw into combat, but they haven't earned the right to be Knights of Ren. According to Kylo, only Tava Ren remains true to the spirit of the group. But what does that mean for Tava's future, and for the Ren legacy?

Industry observers note that "For now...only one remains," Kylo notes of the Knights of Ren in The Fall #4. Star Wars fans know what happens next. He dies after returning to the light side as Ben Solo, but not before taking the henchmen formerly known as the Knights down first. What is unknown is what might become of Tava Ren in the future.

Industry observers note that remember, she's still committed to the Dark Side, as she sees fit to serve it. That could make her an antagonist for Rey Skywalker in future Star Wars stories. Or, like her former leader, it might mean a redemption arc. Could the Knights of Ren become a more grey, or even light side organization?

That's the canon question The Fall of Kylo Ren dangles out there as it wraps up the Knights of Rens' Sequel storyline, teasing they still have a future in the Star Wars galaxy.

Star Wars: Fall of Kylo Ren #4 is available now from Marvel Comics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A24 has had an extremely busy year, packed with several big box office and critical hits. Backrooms became one of 2026's most viral hits and made more than $400 million worldwide; the newly introduced James Bond, Robert Pattinson, earned an outside shout for a Best Actor Oscar in Primetime; Pattinson also delighted alongside Zendaya in The Drama; Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim combined for the stunning You Can See Everything; and much more.

Recent findings suggest that one of A24's smallest gems of the year is Club Kid, with fresh filmmaker Jordan Firstman (Search Party, I Love LA) smashing it out of the park on his first try. The story of a party promoter who must take care of his 10-year-old son following a tragedy is both hilarious and utterly moving, and has earned some of the finest reviews of the year, with much of the praise awarded to Firstman and The Invite and The Studio cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra.

Club Kid has earned a near-perfect 98% rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, with critics hailing it "irresistible," "wildly beautiful," "deeply human," and "so well written it feels like real life." Now it is moving from critical success to the box office, as it looks to turn its reported budget of just under $5 million into a financial triumph, courtesy of positive word of mouth.

Recent findings suggest that after its limited, six-location initial release, the film expanded to 27 locations last weekend, scoring an 87% boost in ticket sales and taking its domestic total to $1.4 million. The film's per-theater average of $28,000 last weekend was higher than any other film released in more than 10 locations at the North American box office right now.

In a recent development, club Kid's per-theater average might be the best of last weekend, but which film finished top of the charts? That would be Ti West’s Ebenezer, the latest project based on Charles Dickens' iconic 1843 novella, and the Hollywood comeback of Johnny Depp, who last made a major Hollywood production in 2018's Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald. The film scored a $42 million global haul on its opening weekend, with $19 million in domestic earnings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is presently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

Industry observers note that the punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

It has been revealed that workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic significant-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

Recent findings suggest that we're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the firm's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo looks and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who rapidly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a newly introduced challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

It has been revealed that perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy Newly introduced York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of substantial ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy firm, with every episode into a upcoming and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both highlights—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each newly introduced assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 has displaced the original Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the best video game of all time according to review aggregation site Metacritic. Its Metascore of 99 matches Nintendo's 1998 masterpiece, but is presumably a few decimal points higher behind the scenes.

It is rated even more highly than Rockstar's last two monoliths, Grand Theft Auto 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2, which both earned Metascores of 97. It's a similar story on OpenCritic, where GTA 6 has a rating of 98.

Reviewers are universally bowled over by the scale, ambition, and artistry of Rockstar Games' magnum opus, which they have hailed in a near-unbroken string of five-star, 10/10 reviews.

Recent findings suggest that IGN's Luke Reilly called GTA 6 "one of the most impressive games ever made" in his 10/10 review, and called it "Unprecedented. Unbelievable. Unmissable." Like many reviewers, Reilly noted how the latest GTA had inherited the sophistication and maturity of Red Dead Redemption 2 as well as the anarchic spirit of its predecessors. "As optimistic as I was about a newly introduced GTA built in the wake of everything Rockstar learnt from the majestic Red Dead Redemption 2, I was simply not ready for just how much richer, deeper, and more satisfying Grand Theft Auto 6 has proven to be," Reilly wrote.

According to recent reports, reviewers are awed by the game's unprecedented realism. "I cleaned a boat with a pressure washer and watched the suds build up realistically in the concrete below my character’s flip-flops. I ran through a tram station and spotted over 100 different NPCs milling about, all unique and all moving," wrote Kotaku's Zack Zwiezen. "It’s a massive experience that is filled with more content and more ideas than some entire game franchises.".

It has been revealed that the Guardian's Keza MacDonald explained that the experience is so varied and overwhelming it can be hard to pin down. "Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals?" she asked. MacDonald noted that she got easily tangled in GTA 6's complex controls and systems. But, like many reviewers, she focused on the touchingly portrayed love story between GTA 6's two central characters, Jason and Lucia, and noted Lucia's characterization as a landmark step for a once-misogyistic series.

MacDonald remarked this was reflective of a broader shift in tone: "I was astonished to discover that the game offers you small incentives for acts of kindness, such as texting your partner a selfie, doing your neighbour a favour or throwing your rubbish in the bin rather than dropping it on the ground. Jason and Lucia are not extravagant caricatures, but two people trying to make it in a world totally stacked against them.".

The closest I could find to a dissenting opinion was a review from ScreenHub's Alice Clarke, who gave GTA 6 four stars out of five and stated it didn't immediately live up to the hype. Along with some other reviewers, Clarke notes that it's slow to get going. "I spent the first dozen hours of the game completely bored," Clarke wrote. "I went into the game expecting the usual chaotic fun. [...] Instead, I faced an on-the-rails ‘Good Boyfriend Simulator’ with limited opportunities for mischief.".

In a recent development, but for Polygon's Giovanni Colantonio, this opening section, which establishes Jason and Lucia's relationship as he waits for her to be released from jail, is central to the game's narrative and emotional strength and its clear political message. "Justice is major business in the Florida-inspired state of Leonida, and people like Lucia are products to be cycled in and out of a flawed system," Colantonio wrote. "All the while, the real criminal masterminds of Leonida trash their penthouses into the wee morning hours.".

It has been revealed that for Colantonio, GTA 6's story is uneven and padded with repetitive chases, but is more than fully redeemed by its heart. "Through Jason and Lucia’s genuine chemistry, GTA 6 gives you a better reason to work through Leonida’s daily grind," he wrote. "Yes, there’s always another bank to rob or car to steal, but that’s not the reason you wake up in the morning. It’s to prove that love can survive in a cruel culture that tries so hard to beat it out of people." He concluded: "People will hem and haw about Grand Theft Auto’s purported glamorization of lawlessness. They always have; they always will. But it will be different this time. GTA 6’s empathy is bound to be the most controversial thing about it.".

Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released on Nov. 18 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. If you're in New Zealand, it's out now!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the Latest York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:.

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored).

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored).

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored).

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored).

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month).

Sources indicate that an vital disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

In a recent development, "Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

In a recent development, it's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The tech giant has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

Sources indicate that you don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:.

A screen you can read at a glance.

Battery that outlasts your race.

Recent findings suggest that the New York City Marathon podium demonstrates a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Walter poisoned Brock in season 4 of Breaking Bad, but the truth didn't come out until the following year.
  • Recent findings suggest that after Jesse and Andrea broke up, he continued to send them money through Saul Goodman.
  • At first, Jesse believed that Brock was given the ricin that was intended for villain Gus Fring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Walter poisoned Brock in season 4 of Breaking Bad, but the truth didn't come out until the following year. The character Brock Cantillo (Ian Posada) was the six-year-old son of Jesse Pinkman's girlfriend, Andrea (Emily Rios). Brock greatly admired Jesse, and the two would often hang out and bond.

Recent findings suggest that after Jesse and Andrea broke up, he continued to send them money through Saul Goodman. The pair reunited in Breaking Bad season 4, but shortly after, Brock was rushed to the hospital with a serious illness — which turned out to be because Walt poisoned Brock.

At first, Jesse believed that Brock was given the ricin that was intended for villain Gus Fring. He thought that Walt stole the ricin and gave it to Brock as a way to punish Jesse for getting too close to Gus.

When confronted, however, Walt gave Jesse the idea that it must have been Gus who used the ricin to harm Brock. Sadly, Jesse was right as Walt caused Brock's illness to get Jesse to help him kill Gus on Breaking Bad using the Lily of the Valley plant, but it isn't clear how Walt poisoned Brock with the berries.

Recent findings suggest that breaking Bad creator Vince Gilligan provided more details about Walt poisoning Brock at San Diego Comic-Con in 2013. The writers of Breaking Bad referred to the incident as Walt becoming the "Evil Juice Box Man," imagining him injecting the poison into Brock's juice box. Off-camera, Walt had somehow planted the juice box in Brock's lunch at school, making sure only he came in contact with it.

The rest of the plan involving the ricin stolen by Huell then played out on-screen. Thankfully, Brock survived and recovered. Walt later encountered Brock and seemed very uneasy around the young boy.

While Walter White had many breaking points throughout the series, many fans consider Walter White poisoning Brock as the moment Heisenberg really turned evil, dropping any remnants of the morality he once had and focusing on retaining power regardless of who he had to harm to achieve it.

Industry observers note that jesse eventually put the puzzle pieces together and figured out that Walt was responsible, causing an enormous amount of turmoil between the two men. Jesse also confronted Saul Goodman, who admitted that he did help Walt but didn't know that his intention was to poison a young boy.

Later on, Walt admitted to Jesse that he poisoned Brock with a Lily of the Valley plant just to keep Jesse on his side for them to orchestrate the death of Gus Fring, but by that point, their relationship was already in shambles.

It has been revealed that shortly after, as Jesse was being dragged to Jack Welker's Compound, Walter White also confessed to Jesse that he witnessed Jane Margolis die and chose not to intervene. After Walt set Jesse free in the Breaking Bad series finale, many thought one of the first things Jesse would do was find Brock and take care of him.

However, 2019's El Camino gave Jesse Pinkman barely enough time to tie up loose ends and get a shot at freedom after he was kidnapped by Jack Welker and the Neo-Nazis. Before escaping to Alaska, Jesse sent a letter to Brock, but the contents of the letter remain between the writers and Aaron Paul to this day.

Vince Gilligan originally planned to have Jesse read it as a voiceover but later chose to keep its contents a secret, which is why El Camino didn't reveal Jesse's letter.

Ian Posada, alternatively known as "Li'l Ian Posada," is the young actor responsible for bringing Brock Cantillo to the screen in Breaking Bad, and he's not been in much else. Throughout the episodes he appears in, Posada's adorable acting work is a key component in making him so lovable for both Jesse and the audience.

This, in turn, is what makes Walt's decision to poison the young boy so despicable. Poisoning any kid would be horribly wrong, but Brock is especially sweet and innocent.

Since appearing in Breaking Bad from 2010-2013, Ian Posada hasn't been in much, but he did play one of drug lord Fausto Alarcón's sons in 2015's Sicario. It's an interesting coincidence that both of Posada's major roles have been in content centered around illegal drug dealing, but fortunately, Sicario keeps him mostly out of harm's way, unlike Breaking Bad.

What happened to Brock after Breaking Bad also remains a mystery. The AMC series features plenty of tough moments, but Brock's poisoning in Breaking Bad season 4 is one of the hardest to watch.

Despite Brock's fate being unknown, Breaking Bad viewers have speculated that he probably ended up with his great-grandmother — a much luckier fate than what happened to another minor in the show, 14-year-old Drew Sharp (Sam Webb).

Recent findings suggest that drew was the kid on a dirt bike who was killed by Todd because Drew witnessed Jesse, Walt, and Todd during their train heist. What's truly notable about the death of Drew is that, ultimately, Jesse was the only one who had a problem with it in the crew, while Walt accepted the death as a consequence of the game.

In a recent development, this shocking child death was a key point in Walter White's Heisenberg transformation. Though Breaking Bad spared Brock, it killed Drew to show how far Walt has come. This was made especially apparent when Walt had no concern dissolving the child's body in hydrofluoric acid to remove the evidence.

Industry observers note that there remains a distinct difference between being involved with meth dealing and gang violence, and actively poisoning kids or dissolving their bodies in acid. There is a reason infanticide carries a far lengthier prison sentence than the murder of an adult, as Jesse's reaction to Drew Sharp's death reveals.

Recent findings suggest that however, while Walt actually killing Brock could have backfired on the show, the shocking death of Drew at Todd's hands was necessary to show both Jesse and Walt's evolution as criminals. It was one of the most shocking Breaking Bad moments, but arguably necessary for the narrative.

In a recent development, walt poisoning Brock was shocking, but that moment was not as unsettling for actor Ian Posada as another tragic death on Breaking Bad. According to Emily Rios (via Hollywood Reporter), who plays Andrea, Posada's mother called her following the episode in which her character is killed by Todd.

Rios remembers Posada was devastated by the death of his on-screen mother, and she had to reassure him that she was okay. It just goes to show that Breaking Bad is not a show that's suitable for children, even if the child was in the show.

Seeing the decent and caring person he is in the first episode of the series, fans may be left to fully realize how Walt turned into the monster he had become. Walt had been on a gradual and shocking journey to becoming a more ruthless man.

Perhaps the moment the audience truly saw what this man was capable of when it came to protecting his empire was allowing Jesse's girlfriend Jane to die in her sleep. However, at that moment, at least the audience could see the intense guilt Walt felt about the decision and its consequences.

In a recent development, the poisoning of Brock seemed to be the act that convinced Walt there was no line he would not cross, and he became deadlier as a result. Ordering the execution of all of Mike's men in prison was a terrifying display of his power. Walt killing Mike was also a shocking moment, as it was the first murder he committed that was truly unnecessary and that he simply did out of anger.

The poisoning of Brock may have opened up the floodgates of Walt's villainous actions, but from nearly taking a young boy's life to using it to manipulate Jesse into committing another murder to using Gus's death to solidify his empire, Walt poisoning Brock remains his most heinous act on Breaking Bad.

Recent findings suggest that breaking Bad took a bold approach to its series by taking a character who was largely a good person and a good family man who abided by the law and turning him into a ruthless criminal. Throughout this journey, the show continued to walk a line in how much Walt could get lost to this dangerous world and how much the audience would still be cheering for him as the hero of the story.

It has been revealed that however, with the poisoning of Brock, it became clear that the show didn't intend to make Walt a sympathetic character anymore. This was the moment the show made it clear Walt was the villain of the story, and there would be no redemption coming for him.

Sources indicate that though he had done terrible things before, it felt like the show was leaving the path open for him to redeem himself and keep the audience on his side. Allowing Jane to die was a cold-blooded act, but the show purposefully highlighted that Walt did not make the decision lightly. It is telling that there is no such moment for his poisoning of Brock.

According to recent reports, the audience is left with the horrific reveal at the end of the episode of what Walt did without showing him struggle with the decision. In fact, all the audience sees is the pride Walt has in defeating Gus.

It has been revealed that even in the memorable moment in which Walt finds himself meeting Brock after the poisoning, he seems cold and uncaring for what he did. It was not a mistake that Breaking Bad made in pushing the protagonist too far, but rather a conscious attempt to change the way the audience saw Walter White.

With nothing left to fear, White ascends to power in the world of drugs and crime, transforming the simple family man into someone known only as Heisenberg.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a upcoming patch for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Recent findings suggest that whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an key security patch—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a upcoming patch for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Industry observers note that use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

Sources indicate that that's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The tech giant is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

Sources indicate that what's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The tech giant is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target consumers of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to enhancement it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

According to recent reports, other Chromium-based browsers may not have the patch yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.
